probes.query: I discarded a long stretch of old operation history and then ran the storage-cleanup command with its expiry set to the present moment. Trace how commits that only the discarded history referenced end up deleted from the underlying Git store. Cover: how the discard step changes the stored history so that the commit index forgets those commits, which operation and view records the cleanup keeps, how the set of surviving commits is derived and pinned against Git's own pruning, and how Git's pruning is finally run and with what cutoff.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: The discard step (cmd_op_abandon) calls op_walk::reparent_range, which writes copies of every descendant operation with rewritten parent lists (attached to the destination operation), so those operations get new operation IDs and the old ones become unreachable.

CRITICAL: The default index store keys its saved index by operation ID (op_links directory). The new head operation has no saved link, so get_index_at_op falls back to build_index_at_operation, which starts from the nearest ancestor operation that has a link (for example the root operation) and indexes only commits referenced by the surviving operations, so commits referenced only by discarded operations are never re-indexed.

build_index_at_operation collects heads from Operation::all_referenced_commit_ids (which includes the predecessor commits recorded by the operation) plus each operation's View::all_referenced_commit_ids.

The cleanup command (cmd_util_gc) requires the head operation, uses a two-week cutoff by default (only the value 'now' is accepted to override), and calls the operation store's gc with the current operation as the only head, then GitBackend::gc with the current index.

SimpleOpStore::gc walks operations depth-first from the head to find reachable operations and their views, then deletes operation and view files that are not reachable unless their modification time is newer than the cutoff.

GitBackend::gc takes index.all_heads_for_gc() (heads of all indexed commits, excluding the root commit), rewrites the refs under refs/jj/keep/<commit id> via recreate_no_gc_refs (deleting other keep refs unless the loose ref is newer than the cutoff), garbage-collects the extra-metadata table segments, and then runs git gc through the configured Git executable with a prune cutoff of the form @<unix seconds> +0000.

probes.query: I have several unrelated fixes sitting in my working-copy commit, and each touches lines that were last changed in a different earlier commit of my stack. I want jj to push every fix back into the commit where its lines were last modified, automatically. How does it decide which earlier commits are eligible by default, how does it work out which commit each changed line belongs to (and how is the per-file history lookup kept cheap), which kinds of changes does it refuse or leave behind, how is a moved change combined with the receiving commit, and under what condition does my original commit disappear afterwards?
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: By default the receiving commits are the mutable ones: the destination argument defaults to the mutable() revset, defined in revsets.toml as ~immutable(), where immutable() is ::(immutable_heads() | root()); only ancestors of the source are considered, and the chosen targets are checked with check_rewritable.

CRITICAL: split_hunks_to_trees annotates the parent-side text of each changed file (FileAnnotator::with_file_content, computed with the destinations as the domain); annotate::process_commits builds the revset heads | (domain & ancestors(heads)) filtered by the File predicate for that path, walks the graph, and propagates line identity to parents through a line diff (copy_same_lines_with using ContentDiff::by_line). Lines with unresolved origin are dropped when annotation ranges are built.

The File predicate in the default revset engine uses the changed-path index (index.changed_paths()) when the commit is covered, and otherwise falls back to diffing the commit against its parents (has_diff_from_parent) with the file matcher.

split_file_hunks moves a modification or insertion only if its left range lies wholly inside one annotation range, and treats a pure insertion exactly between two annotation ranges as ambiguous (left behind); a pure deletion may span several contiguous annotation ranges and is split among them.

Paths that are new files are skipped silently; symlinks, conflicted files, Git submodules and access-denied files are reported as skipped with a reason (to_file_value); a file deletion is propagated only for a destination whose selected hunks delete the entire file content.

absorb_hunks runs transform_descendants: each receiving commit is rebased and its tree becomes a three-way MergedTree::merge of (its tree, the source's parent tree, the tree with the selected hunks) with absorb-specific labels, and the source commit is added to its predecessors; the source commit is reparented (hunks removed) and abandoned only if is_discardable() (no changes left and an empty description).

probes.query: I turned on commit signing in my configuration but never run any dedicated signing command. Trace how a commit that jj writes or rewrites ends up carrying a cryptographic signature inside the Git object. Cover: which rule decides whether a given commit gets signed (and how that changes when someone else authored it or it was already signed), how the signing program is chosen among the supported ones, how the signing key is picked when none is given for the GPG family versus SSH, where in the Git commit the signature is stored, and how pushing treats commits that are not signed yet.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: SignSettings::should_sign (settings.rs) decides per commit from the configured behavior: drop never signs; keep signs only if the commit already has a signature and its author email equals the user email; own signs whenever the author email equals the user email; force always signs. The default behavior is keep and the default backend is none (lib/src/config/misc.toml).

CRITICAL: commit_builder::write_to_store signs only if store.signer().can_sign() (a main backend is configured) and should_sign is true; it clears the commit's old secure_sig and passes a signing closure (Signer::sign with an optional per-commit key override) into Store::write_commit.

The Signer is built when the repo loader is initialized from the file system (RepoLoader::init_from_file_system in repo.rs calls signing_factory::signer_from_settings): it instantiates the GPG, GPGSM and SSH backends (plus a test one), picks the main backend by the configured backend name (none means no main backend, an unknown name is an error), and keeps the others only for verification.

Default key when no override is given: GPG uses the configured signing key, falling back to the user email; GPGSM always falls back to the user email; SSH uses the configured signing key and returns a MissingKey error if there is none.

GitBackend::write_commit serializes the commit, calls the signing closure on those bytes, and stores the signature as an extra commit header whose name depends on the Git hash kind (signature_field_name), and keeps the signed data in the commit's secure signature.

On push, when the sign-on-push setting is on (default false), sign_commits_before_push forces the 'own' behavior, signs only mutable unsigned commits authored by the user (reparenting descendants and remapping the pushed ref updates), and warns about immutable commits that need a signature but are skipped.

probes.query: When I divide a commit by choosing changes in an external graphical program that I named in my configuration, how does jj hand that program the before and after content and take the edited result back? Cover: how the configured name becomes a program plus argument list (and what happens when the name is not a configured tool, or no editor is configured at all), what decides whether the program is shown two folders or three, which files are placed on disk and which sides are made read-only, where the instruction text for the user goes and when it is removed, how a tool that has to be started once per file differs, and how the edited folder becomes the new tree.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: DiffEditor::from_settings reads the editor setting (ui.diff-editor) through editor_args_from_settings; if it is unset it prints a hint and uses the builtin editor. A string value that names a built-in or a [merge-tools.<name>] entry is resolved via DiffEditTool::get_tool_config / get_external_tool_config (program defaults to the tool name); otherwise the value is treated as a literal command line, split into a program and arguments (ExternalMergeTool::with_edit_args; with no arguments the default left/right arguments apply). An explicitly requested tool name that is not configured is run as a program of that name with default arguments. An external tool whose edit arguments are empty is rejected.

CRITICAL: edit_diff_external decides two-way versus three-way by scanning the edit arguments for an output variable (find_all_variables): present means the tool gets left, right and an editable output folder (DiffType::ThreeWay), absent means only left and right with the right folder being edited. Arguments are expanded with interpolate_variables.

check_out_trees checks out the before and after trees into temporary directories (with a state directory each) using a sparse pattern that contains only the changed files matching the matcher; the left side is made read-only, and in the three-way case the right side is read-only too.

DiffEditWorkingCopies::check_out writes the instruction text to a JJ-INSTRUCTIONS file in the editable folder (output, or right in the two-way case) only if the instructions setting is on and no such file already exists; snapshot_results deletes that file before snapshotting.

The ExternalMergeTool default edit invocation mode is Dir (one run with folder variables); with FileByFile the tool is started once for each checked-out file with per-file variables (working_copies.checked_out_files()).

snapshot_results snapshots the editable folder's tree state (output if present, else right) with an everything matcher and no size limit, and its current tree is returned as the edited tree; DiffSelector::select first restores the selected changes and skips the editor with a warning if the diff is empty.

probes.query: A local bookmark follows a branch on a remote only once that remote branch is marked as tracked. Apart from running the explicit command that starts tracking, in which situations does jj mark a remote branch as tracked by itself? Name each situation, the setting (if there is one) that controls it, and the function that makes the decision.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: When Git refs are imported (fetch, import, colocated sync), a remote bookmark seen for the first time starts tracked only if its remote is the internal local-Git pseudo-remote or its name matches that remote's configured auto-track matcher, otherwise it starts untracked; tags always start tracked. This is default_remote_ref_state_for (lib/git.rs), fed by GitImportOptions.remote_auto_track_bookmarks, which load_git_import_options builds with parse_remote_auto_track_bookmarks_map from the per-remote settings (RemoteSettings).

CRITICAL: Creating a bookmark, or setting one that is new, starts tracking it on every remote whose matcher matches its name, where the matcher is the union of the auto-track-bookmarks and auto-track-created-bookmarks expressions (parse_remote_auto_track_bookmarks_map_for_new_bookmarks) and tracking uses MutableRepo::track_remote_bookmark; a warning is printed if the bookmark already exists on that remote.

When cloning, the remote's default branch is tracked, but only if the chosen working branch is the default branch and the Git setting for tracking the default bookmark on clone is on (default true in misc.toml).
Exporting local bookmarks to Git records them in the view as tracked entries of the internal Git pseudo-remote (copy_exportable_local_bookmarks_to_remote_view in lib/git.rs).
After a successful push, push_refs records each pushed bookmark and tag in the remote view with state Tracked.

Renaming a bookmark carries tracking over: for each remote where the old bookmark was tracked, the new name is tracked, unless an untracked remote bookmark with the new name already exists (a warning is printed and tracking is dropped).

probes.query: Besides the commands whose job is to hide commits, in what situations does jj on its own remove a commit from visible history? I mean side effects of moving the working copy away from a commit, of picking up changes made through Git, and of reconciling concurrent operations. For each situation, name the function that decides it and the exact condition, and say where the controlling setting (if any) gets its default and how it reaches the decision.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: When the working copy leaves a commit (MutableRepo::edit and check_out), maybe_abandon_wc_commit abandons the old working-copy commit only if Commit::is_discardable (no changes relative to its parents and an empty description), no other workspace's working copy, local bookmark or local tag points at it, and it is a visible head.

CRITICAL: On Git ref import, import_refs_inner calls abandon_unreachable_commits only when the abandon-unreachable setting is on and some previously imported heads existed; it hides visible commits that were reachable from the old referenced heads but are not pinned by local bookmarks/tags, untracked visible remote refs, or the root.
The abandon-unreachable setting defaults to true in lib/src/config/misc.toml, is read into GitSettings (lib/git.rs) and reaches the import through load_git_import_options in cli/src/git_util.rs.
Commits that the import identifies as rewritten (through synthetic predecessors based on change ID) are removed from the abandoned list afterwards (abandoned_commits.retain).

When concurrent operations are merged (RepoLoader::merge_operations, triggered on divergent operation heads), MutableRepo::merge_view calls record_rewrites for the heads removed on each side, but only when the repo is backed by the default index; a removed commit whose change ID has no new visible commit is recorded as abandoned, one new commit makes it a plain rewrite, several make it a divergent rewrite.
With a non-default index, merge_view just removes the base heads that the other side dropped, with no abandon or rewrite bookkeeping.

probes.query: When I ask for a diff, or for a log with patches, what decides which output format I get? Explain the interplay of: several format options given together; an option that names an external program or a built-in format; no option at all; the configured default (which can be a built-in format name, the name of a configured external tool, or a literal command line); and how default values for context lines and for word-level alternation are layered with command-line values. Say which combinations are errors.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: DiffFormatArgs places the short formats (summary, stat, types, name-only) in one mutually exclusive clap group and the long formats (git, color-words) in another, so at most one of each can be requested; diff_formats_for returns the requested formats, and only if none was requested does it fall back to default_diff_format.

CRITICAL: The tool option (diff_formats_from_args) accepts either ':<builtin>' (placed in the short or long slot by kind) or an external tool name; an external tool always occupies the long slot, and it is an error (ensure_new) if that slot, or the same builtin's slot, was already requested by another option.

default_diff_format reads the configured default (ui.diff-formatter, default ':color-words'): a string starting with ':' must be a builtin name (else a config type error); another string is looked up as a configured tool (diff_formatter_tool, which errors if the tool has no diff arguments, i.e. cannot be used for diff formatting); a string that is not a configured tool or any non-string value (a command array) is used as a literal command via ExternalMergeTool::with_diff_args.

For log-like commands (diff_formats_for_log) the list may be empty; the patch option adds the default format as the long format when none was requested, unless the requested short format equals that default.

Each builtin format takes its defaults from settings (diff.color-words.context/max-inline-alternation/conflict, diff.git.context/show-path-prefix) and then merge_args overrides context and whitespace-ignore options from the command line; the max-inline-alternation value -1 means unlimited and other negative values are a type error.

probes.query: I wrote a command alias inside a config block that applies only to one subcommand, and another alias that I pass on the command line as a config override. Neither alias works, although aliases in my plain user config do. Why? Explain at which points during startup the configuration is built, which facts about the environment are known at each point (repository, subcommand, directory given on the command line), how aliases and the default command are expanded, how the scoped blocks are matched, and what jj prints when the expansion would come out differently.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: Aliases and the default command are expanded (expand_args: resolve_aliases, resolve_default_command, resolve_aliases again) using the config resolved at the first stage of run_internal, which has system, user, and (if the current directory is inside a workspace) repo and workspace layers, but no subcommand name and no --config layers.

CRITICAL: A scoped block conditioned on commands cannot match at that stage, because the resolution context's command is None and matches_command returns false when candidates exist but the command is unknown; the command name is only set later by ConfigEnv::set_command_name(command_name(&matches)) after clap parsing, as the space-joined subcommand chain.

Command-line --config/--config-file layers (and the color/quiet/no-pager overrides) are extracted by parse_early_args from the already expanded arguments, added to the raw config and re-resolved afterwards, so aliases inside them are not seen; warn_if_args_mismatch re-expands the arguments with the new config and prints a warning that aliases cannot be loaded from the repository path or config arguments if the result differs.

If the repository option is given, the workspace loader is recreated, the repo and workspace paths are reset and their configs reloaded, and the final resolve (applying workspace config, command-line config and the commands condition) runs only afterwards; migration of deprecated keys runs after every resolve and only the last migration messages are printed.

Matching rules in lib config_resolver: a commands entry matches if the actual command equals it or starts with it followed by a space (so 'foo' matches 'foo bar' but 'foo bar' does not match 'foo'); repositories/workspaces entries match as path prefixes of the repo path (<root>/.jj/repo) or workspace path, with a leading ~ expanded using the home directory, and fail if the path is unknown; resolve() flattens scope tables into following layers of the same source, in order.

probes.query: A GraphQL schema author marks a list-of-decimals field as a stored vector and asks for nearest-neighbour search on it, writing the search option text so that it sets only the one tuning value that controls how quickly the number of graph layers scales. Follow that option text from the GraphQL schema to the point where an index object exists. Which step first rejects an unknown option name or an unsupported distance-measure name, how does the engine find the index implementation from its name, and what values do the layer-count, build-effort, search-effort and distance-measure settings take when they are left out?
expectedFacts: The GraphQL layer (graphql/schema/rules.go) parses the option text as name-colon-value pairs in YAML style (parseSearchOptions) and getSearchOptions rewrites it in DQL syntax with sorted keys and every value quoted; an empty or null value or unbalanced parentheses make the argument invalid, and the vector search argument is allowed only when the field also carries the embedding directive. It does not check option names or values.

graphql/schema/schemagen.go getAllSearchIndexes appends the rewritten options to the index name, the embedding field gets the Dgraph type float32vector, and the generated Dgraph schema line prints the index as @index(<name>(<options>)).

The admin schema-update resolver (graphql/admin/schema.go) passes the generated Dgraph schema (DGSchema) to edgraph.UpdateGQLSchema, which runs parseSchemaFromAlterOperation (schema.ParseWithNamespace) in the Alpha before any proposal reaches the cluster.

CRITICAL: schema/parse.go parseTokenOrVectorIndexSpec is where an unknown option name or an unsupported distance-measure value is first rejected: it looks the name up in the tok index-factory registry (GetIndexFactory), requires a vector-typed predicate, and calls AllowedOptions().GetParsedOption for every pair; the result is stored as a VectorIndexSpec (name plus option pairs).

The registry is filled in tok/tok.go init() with the HNSW persistent factory (registerIndexFactory(createIndexFactory(hnsw.CreateFactory...))); its AllowedOptions (tok/hnsw/persistent_factory.go) declares four integer options (exponent, maxLevels, efConstruction, efSearch) plus a custom metric option that accepts only euclidean, cosine or dotproduct.

CRITICAL: Defaults are applied when the index object is created (FactoryCreateSpec.CreateIndex -> CreateOrReplace -> persistentHNSW.applyOptions): if exponent is given, any missing maxLevels = exponent, efConstruction = 50 x exponent and efSearch = 30 x exponent; with nothing given the values are 3, 150 and 90; a missing metric means euclidean.

probes.query: A replica of a data group was offline so long that its peers have discarded the log entries it needs. After it rejoins, how does it catch up? Cover what makes it start, what it does to its own server state before copying, how it finds the peer to copy from, how much data it asks for and which rule the sending side uses to decide which stored entries to send, and what the receiver must clean up and reload afterwards.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: The trigger is a Raft ready batch carrying a non-empty snapshot in node.Run (worker/draft.go); a snapshot whose Raft context id is the node's own is ignored. Otherwise the node marks itself unhealthy, drains the apply channel and waits for the applied mark before it fetches data, and retries the fetch every second until it succeeds; only then the Raft snapshot is saved to storage.
The requested SinceTs is the ReadTs of the node's own current snapshot, or 0 (full copy) when no snapshot can be read.

node.retrieveSnapshot (as the opSnapshot task, which cancels rollups) takes the peer address from the snapshot's Raft context and falls back to leaderBlocking (membership state) when no connection exists, then runs populateSnapshot.

CRITICAL: On the sending side (grpcWorker.StreamSnapshot / doStreamSnapshot in worker/snapshot.go) the peer waits until its posting oracle has reached the snapshot ReadTs, streams from a Badger stream at that timestamp, and its key chooser sends only versions at or above SinceTs plus schema and type keys (which always sit at version 1); at the end it sends the full lists of predicates and types.
populateSnapshot writes with a Badger StreamWriter (replacing data) when SinceTs is 0, and with a managed write batch when SinceTs is non-zero (incremental).

After the stream, deleteStalePreds removes predicates and types that the sender no longer lists, posting.ResetCache clears the in-memory lists, an ACK is sent, x.VerifySnapshot runs only in debug-tagged builds, and retrieveSnapshot reloads the schema (schema.LoadFromDb) and triggers a membership sync; a sender-side failure is reported to Raft as a snapshot failure.

probes.query: After the cluster coordinator decides that a client transaction commits, how does every replica of the data groups that hold its writes learn the outcome and make the data visible? Follow the decision from the coordinator's own replicated log to the moment a reader that was waiting for that point in time is released: who streams the outcome, which replica turns it into a replicated entry, what ordering rule applies, what is written to disk, and what finally wakes the waiting reader.
expectedFacts: In the coordinator, Server.commit assigns the commit timestamp and Server.proposeTxn proposes the transaction status through the coordinator's own Raft; when that entry is applied (dgraph/cmd/zero/raft.go) Oracle.updateCommitStatus pushes a one-transaction delta onto the updates channel.

Oracle.sendDeltasToSubscribers merges queued deltas and sends the batch to every subscriber only once the done-watermark has reached the largest commit timestamp in it (so commits are never sent out of order); a subscriber whose channel is full is closed and removed. Server.Oracle streams these deltas (new subscribers first get the full current state) with the group checksums added.

CRITICAL: Only each group's Raft leader consumes the stream (groupi.processOracleDeltaStream in worker/groups.go): it batches deltas, sorts transactions by commit timestamp, and proposes pb.Proposal{Delta} through the group's own Raft with unlimited retry; followers never apply the stream directly, they apply the replicated entry.

When the Delta entry is applied (worker/draft.go applyCommitted -> node.commitOrAbort), each committed transaction's deltas are written to disk with Txn.CommitToDisk (exponential retry, then flush), the group checksum is stored, cached lists touched by the transaction are updated, and posting.Oracle().ProcessDelta is called.

CRITICAL: posting/oracle.go ProcessDelta removes the pending transactions, queues the keys of committed ones for rollup, and, only if the delta's MaxAssigned is not below the current one, closes every waiter channel whose timestamp is at or below MaxAssigned and stores the new MaxAssigned; WaitForTs (called by reads such as worker/task.go processTask) returns when its channel is closed.

probes.query: A client sends the GraphQL API a read request for one of the generated look-up-one-object-by-identifier queries. Follow it from the schema-level classification of that request to the JSON handed back: how does the server decide which handler runs it, how is it turned into the database query language and who is given the translator, does the database call leave the process, and at which layer is the final GraphQL-shaped JSON produced, with nulls and type names filled in?
expectedFacts: The kind of a generated query is derived from its name in graphql/schema/wrappers.go queryType (a get-prefixed name is the by-identifier look-up kind; other prefixes give filter, aggregate, password-check and similarity kinds; a custom directive gives DQL or HTTP kinds).

graphql/resolve/resolver.go WithConventionResolvers registers, for every query name of those kinds, a constructor returning NewQueryResolver(fns.Qrw, fns.Ex); admin.go resetSchema rebuilds the factory on every schema update from a base factory whose default resolver returns the 'no suitable resolver' error, and queryResolverFor looks the handler up by query name and wraps it with any configured middleware.
The translator and executor come from graphql/admin/admin.go NewServers: Qrw = resolve.NewQueryRewriter() and Ex = resolve.NewDgraphExecutor().

CRITICAL: queryResolver.rewriteAndExecute calls queryRewriter.Rewrite (which switches on the query kind and applies auth rewriting) to get []*dql.GraphQuery, renders them with dgraph.AsString, and runs executor.Execute with a read-only request.

The executor (graphql/dgraph/execute.go DgraphEx) runs in the same process: it sets the IsGraphql context flag and calls edgraph.Server.QueryGraphQL directly, passing the GraphQL field; there is no network hop.

CRITICAL: edgraph doQuery hands qc.gqlField to query.ToJson; toFastJSON uses newGraphQLEncoder (query/outputnode_graphql.go) when a GraphQL field is present, so the query engine itself writes the GraphQL-shaped JSON (nulls, type names); the default completer for these queries is a no-op, and RequestResolver.Resolve runs a request's queries in parallel goroutines.

probes.query: Predicate and type names that start with the engine's own reserved prefix are treated specially in a running cluster (leave out the offline loaders). Where does the code refuse a client's attempt to alter, drop or write them, where does it let some of them through, and where does it instead silently skip or pin them, for example when assigning data to groups, moving or rebalancing data between groups, and emitting change events? Give each location and the rule applied there.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: edgraph/server.go parseSchemaFromAlterOperation rejects a schema alter of a pre-defined predicate or type unless it equals the built-in definition (schema.CheckAndModifyPreDefPredicate / IsPreDefTypeChanged), and rejects any other reserved-prefix predicate or type unless it is owned by a registered reserved namespace (x.IsRegisteredReservedPredicate / IsRegisteredReservedType).

Dropping is refused for pre-defined predicates and types (edgraph/server.go drop-attr and drop-type branches); dropping a value-locked registered predicate needs the owner's trust marker in the context.

CRITICAL: Writes are guarded twice: edgraph/server.go newReservedPredicateGuard (used by validateNQuads) refuses user writes to the GraphQL-reserved predicates unless the request came through the GraphQL admin path, and refuses value-locked registered predicates without the owner's marker; worker/proposal.go node.proposeAndWait refuses a write to a reserved-prefix predicate that has no schema yet unless a registered namespace owns it.

ACL-specific guards: query/mutation.go checkIfDeletingAclOperation refuses deleting the guardians group or the root user node when ACL is on, and edgraph/access.go authorizeMutation refuses changing or deleting the permissions of ACL predicates (even by guardians) and blocks non-allowed namespaces from mutating ACL predicates.

Placement rules in the coordinator: reserved-prefix tablets are forced onto group 1 (dgraph/cmd/zero/zero.go Inform for unknown tablets and ShouldServe), movePredicate refuses to move one, and chooseTablet skips them when rebalancing (dgraph/cmd/zero/tablet.go).
worker/cdc.go toCDCEvent silently skips edges whose predicate is reserved, so no change event is emitted for them.

probes.query: An operator starts a data server with the at-rest symmetric-key feature turned on. Which of the data that this running server writes or reads is protected with that key, and where does each place obtain the key? Also say how the key reaches the server, what restores use instead, and which neighbouring protected output is keyed from an entirely different source.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: The key is loaded at startup by x.GetEncAclKeys (x/acl_enc_keys.go) from the encryption flag's key file or from Vault (both together is an error; the key must be 16, 32 or 64 bytes) and dgraph/cmd/alpha/run.go stores it in x.WorkerConfig.EncryptionKey, which every in-server use below reads.

worker/server_state.go InitStorage opens the main posting store through setBadgerOptions with WithEncryptionKey(x.WorkerConfig.EncryptionKey) and opens the write-ahead log with raftwal.InitEncrypted(Config.WALDir, key).

raftwal (storage.go InitEncrypted sets a package key; log.go openLogFile uses a Badger key registry with a ten-day key rotation, refuses to open an already encrypted log file without a key, and cannot be switched off afterwards).
posting/index.go rebuilder.Run opens its temporary index database with the same key (and larger caches) when the key is set.

Backup output is wrapped with enc.GetWriter(x.WorkerConfig.EncryptionKey, ...) in worker/backup.go WriteBackup, the manifest records Encrypted, and an incremental backup is refused when the latest manifest's encrypted state differs from the server's unless a full backup is forced; export files are wrapped the same way in worker/export.go ExportWriter.open.

CRITICAL: Restores do not use the server's key: worker/online_restore.go getEncConfig builds the key from the request's key-file path (and Vault fields) and restore_map.go uses that key; and the audit log is keyed from a separate audit key file (audit/audit.go readAuditEncKey, the audit flag's own file option), not from the at-rest key.

probes.query: An operator changes the definition of an existing field that already holds data, for example switching its search indexing, its reverse-direction or counting support, or making it multi-valued. Which kinds of change make the server delete and rebuild stored derived data, which only delete it, and which are refused or need nothing? While the background rebuild runs, which definition of the field do ordinary reads see compared with incoming writes, what happens to another definition-change request that arrives meanwhile, and what else on the server changes behaviour?
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: posting/index.go IndexRebuild decides per aspect. Search index: no index before or after means nothing; index removed means delete only; value type changed means delete everything and rebuild; otherwise the tokenizer sets (and vector index specs by name plus options) are diffed, deleting removed ones and rebuilding added ones. Reverse and count: turned on means rebuild, turned off means delete, unchanged means nothing. NeedIndexRebuild is true if any of the three says rebuild.

Scalar to list is a data rewrite run first (BuildData -> rebuildListType re-keys the untagged value by fingerprint); list to scalar is refused (needsListTypeRebuild error, and checkSchema in worker/mutation.go refuses it when edges exist), as are scalar-uid changes while data exists and password type changes.

CRITICAL: While rebuilding, schema.State has two views: reads see the 'query schema' from GetQuerySchema (new definition minus tokenizers pending deletion, with count and reverse switched off while they rebuild), while writes (IsWrite context) see the new definition stored with SetMutSchema; the mutation entry is cleared when done and the old schema restored on failure (undoSchemaUpdate).

runSchemaMutation (worker/mutation.go) starts the rebuild as the opIndexing task (cancelling the rollup task), runs one goroutine per predicate throttled by a Badger-file-based limit, and the leader proposes a snapshot afterwards if the work took at least ten seconds; other group members block in waitForTask(opIndexing) until it finishes.

Another alter request is rejected by edgraph parseSchemaFromAlterOperation with errIndexingInProgress as long as any mutation schema exists (state.IndexingInProgress); Alter sleeps one second before returning so the client waits.
While indexing is in progress posting/list.go skips the fast length shortcut in getPostingAndLengthNoSort and uses the slow path.

probes.query: The storage layer keeps recent edits to an edge list as small layered updates on top of a base list and, in the background, folds them into one complete list. Which events queue a list for folding and with what priority, how are queued lists batched and rate-limited and when can requests be lost, at which timestamp is the folded result written, and which other long-running activities on a data server stop this background job and when does it come back?
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: There are two priority channels. Low priority: Txn.CommitToDisk queues every key it wrote (deferred), and ReadPostingList queues any list it found with deltas. High priority: ReadPostingList and checkForRollup (cache paths) queue a list with more than five hundred deltas, and oracle.ProcessDelta queues the keys of committed transactions.

addKeyToBatch collects keys in a pooled batch and hands it to the channel only at sixteen keys (a comment says sixty-four); the channel holds sixteen batches and a full channel makes it drop the batch (lossy).

Process skips a key rolled up in the last ten seconds (map by key hash, cleaned every five minutes), throttles low-priority batches with a one-millisecond limiter, and a 500 ms ticker also flushes a pending high-priority batch.

rollUpKey takes a fresh read-write timestamp from Zero (State.GetTimestamp), waits until that timestamp has been applied (giving up with ErrHighPriorityOp if the job is cancelled), reads the list at it, calls List.Rollup, removes the key from the cache and writes the result.
List.Rollup writes the folded list at the newest delta's commit timestamp plus one (not at the fresh timestamp), except for a max-timestamp rollup, which keeps the commit timestamp itself.

CRITICAL: The job runs as the opRollup task started at node start in worker/draft.go; startTaskAtTs cancels it for indexing, snapshot (sending and receiving), predicate move, backup and restore (backup and restore cancel every other operation), and when any non-rollup task ends stopTask waits ten seconds and then tries to start rollup again (the error is ignored if another task is running).

probes.author: r3x-tortoise-orm-drafter
probes.query: When rows come back from the database, the library turns some column values into Python values with a conversion routine owned by the field kind, turns others with a plain call of the Python type, and leaves the rest exactly as the driver gave them. Trace where this three-way split is decided, what facts it uses (including what differs between SQLite, PostgreSQL and the remaining engines), how a field kind can ask to skip its own routine, when the decision is computed, and which other kind of query reuses it.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: Model._init_from_db fills each loaded column from one of three precomputed lists on the model meta: db_native_fields (value assigned as the driver returned it), db_default_fields (value passed through the field's Python type unless None) and db_complex_fields (value passed through the field's own to_python_value).

CRITICAL: MetaInfo._generate_db_fields makes the split: a field is native when its field_type is in the executor class's DB_NATIVE set and it either does not override to_python_value or sets skip_to_python_if_native; it is 'default' when it does not override to_python_value; otherwise it is 'complex'.

The DB_NATIVE set is engine specific: the base executor lists bytes, str, int, float, Decimal, datetime and date; the SQLite executor narrows it to bytes, str, int, float; the PostgreSQL-family executor adds bool and UUID to the base set.

Only DecimalField, DateField and TimeField set skip_to_python_if_native to True (the base Field default is False); DatetimeField overrides to_python_value without the flag, so it stays 'complex' on every engine.
The split is computed per model in MetaInfo.finalise_model (via _generate_db_fields), which Apps._build_initial_querysets calls after the connection (and so its executor class) is known.
FieldSelectQuery.resolve_to_python_value returns an identity function for fields in db_native_fields, and the values()/values_list() queries use it when converting result columns.

probes.author: r3x-tortoise-orm-drafter
probes.query: A query asks the library to bring related records along with the main records in a single database round trip. Trace how it works from the request method to the finished objects: where the request is recorded, where and how the join and the extra columns are added, what bookkeeping is kept about the column layout, and how one flat result row is cut back into several objects that are linked to each other. Include what happens when the related row is missing and when the same query also restricts which fields to load.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: QuerySet.select_related only adds the requested names to a set; the joins and extra columns are created later in QuerySet._make_query, which calls _join_select_related for each name after ordering and filters are resolved.

_join_select_related expands the double-underscore path with expand_lookup_expression and joins every hop through _join_table_by_field (get_joins_for_related_field), using a LEFT OUTER JOIN that is de-duplicated through the list of already joined tables.

For each hop it appends a tuple (related model, number of the model's db fields, field name, parent model, path) to _select_related_idx and selects the related columns aliased as '<table alias>.<column>'.
QuerySet._execute passes _select_related_idx to the executor, and BaseExecutor.execute_select slices each flat row into consecutive chunks using the recorded counts.

CRITICAL: For each related chunk execute_select strips the alias prefix (split on the first dot), builds the related object with that model's _init_from_db, finds the parent by path and attaches the object by setting a private underscore-prefixed attribute with object.__setattr__.

If every value in a related chunk is falsy the related object is None (LEFT JOIN found nothing); a count of 0, produced by _resolve_only for a nested only() field, creates an empty placeholder instance; when only() restricts fields, _join_select_related adds no related columns itself.

probes.author: r3x-tortoise-orm-drafter
probes.query: A web application starts the ORM inside the web framework's startup hook, but incoming requests run in different tasks than the startup task, and queries still find the right database connections. Explain end to end how the startup helper asks for this, where the shared fallback is stored and guarded, how a model resolves its connection at request time, and why connections created at startup are visible in another task even though connection storage is per-task.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: RegisterTortoise defaults its global-fallback switch to True (Tortoise.init and TortoiseContext.init default it to False) and init_orm passes it into Tortoise.init, then also stores the context on app.state.

Tortoise.init takes the context from the context variable only; if there is none it creates a TortoiseContext and enters it, which sets the variable in the startup task alone; TortoiseContext.init ends by calling set_global_context(self) when the switch is on, and a second global context raises ConfigurationError.
get_current_context returns the context-variable value first and falls back to the module-level _global_context; require_context raises RuntimeError when neither exists.

A model finds its connection through MetaInfo.db -> get_connection(default_connection) -> require_context().connections.get(alias), so a request task without its own context variable resolves the startup context through the global fallback.

CRITICAL: ConnectionHandler keeps connections in a ContextVar whose default is one shared empty dict; startup creation writes into that default dict without calling set, so other tasks see the same connections, whereas transactions use set() with a copied dict that stays task-local.
Shutdown (close_orm -> Tortoise.close_connections -> TortoiseContext.close_connections) closes the handler and resets _global_context to None when it is that context.

probes.author: r3x-tortoise-orm-drafter
probes.query: After the models are initialised, the library adds relation-related members that the developer never wrote. The migration system must not record them as the developer's own, and must be able to rebuild them later. Name each kind of automatically added member, say how each kind is marked, and list every place that sets the mark, skips such members when snapshotting or writing migration files, reads information back from them, recreates them when migrations are replayed, or skips them when tables are created.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: Apps._init_relations creates three kinds of automatic members: an integer key column named after the foreign key field plus _id whose reference attribute points back at that FK field (apps.py:193), a reverse relation on the target model (BackwardFKRelation or BackwardOneToOneRelation), and for many-to-many a reverse M2M field flagged _generated = True.
CRITICAL: ModelState.make_from_model skips all three kinds when snapshotting: instances of BackwardFKRelation, M2M fields with _generated, and any field whose reference is not None.
MigrationWriter._format_create_model additionally leaves out any field whose name equals another field's source_field, i.e. the generated key column of an FK.

ForeignKeyFieldInstance.deconstruct reads the real column name back from the generated key column (the field named by source_field) so the written file carries the column name the developer asked for.

On replay State._reload re-renders model classes from the states and calls apps._init_relations (StateApps._init_relations defers models whose target is not registered yet), which creates the automatic members again.

The schema editors' _get_m2m_table_definition (base, MySQL, MSSQL, Oracle) return None for a _generated reverse M2M so only the forward side creates the link table, and _get_model_sql_data uses a key column's reference to emit the FK definition.

probes.author: r3x-tortoise-orm-drafter
probes.query: A model declares an index that has a specific kind (for example a text-search or hash kind) and, for some index classes, a row-filter condition. Explain what SQL each of SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and Oracle ends up with for the kind and the condition, both when all tables are created from the model classes and when the index is added by a migration step. Name the code that makes each engine behave differently.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: An Index carries its kind in INDEX_TYPE and a free text in extra; PartialIndex builds extra as ' WHERE col = value AND ...' from its condition dict and FullTextIndex sets extra to ' WITH PARSER <name>'.

Create-all path: BaseSchemaGenerator._get_field_indexes_sqls calls Index.get_sql, which calls _get_index_sql with the kind and extra; the base template (used by SQLite) puts the kind before the INDEX keyword and the extra at the end, so both appear.
PostgreSQL (generator and migration editor) rewrites the kind into 'USING <kind>' placed after the table name and before the column list, and appends the extra, so the WHERE condition is honoured.
CRITICAL: The MSSQL and Oracle index templates have no slot for the kind or the extra (in both the generators and the editors), so both are silently dropped; their generators also force safe=False.

CRITICAL: BulkCreateQuery._execute_many walks each batch from chunk(objects, batch_size) and splits instances by that flag: flagged ones use the 'all' statement with their key value, the others use the plain statement; each non-empty group is sent through the client's execute_many, so one batch can produce two statements (sql() joins both with a semicolon for a mix).

probes.author: r3x-typedoc-drafter
probes.query: A monorepo is documented one package at a time and the per-package results are combined afterwards. Package A's public API mentions a class declared in package B. While A is being documented, the compiler sees B only through its compiled declaration files, which carry source maps back to B's TypeScript. After the combine step, A's mention of that class is a working link into B's own documentation, even though every internal numeric identifier was reassigned. Trace how the class's identity is formed when the mention is first converted (including why the location of the compiled output does not matter), how that identity is saved, and how it is matched up again after loading. Then say which code decides whether the mention is drawn as a link on a page.
expectedFacts: Converting a type mention creates an unresolved ReferenceType that carries a ReflectionSymbolId (referenceConverter -> Context.createSymbolReference -> createSymbolId -> createSymbolIdImpl), not a pointer to a reflection, because B is not part of A's project.

CRITICAL: The identity is package name + package-relative path + qualified name. The path part comes from the original source file found by mapping the compiled declaration file through resolveDeclarationMaps (it reads the sibling .map file, takes the first of its sources joined with any source root). The mapping cache is pre-filled by addInferredDeclarationMapPaths, called from getEntryPrograms for the root program and every referenced project, so the identity does not depend on where compiled output lives. The package name is taken from findPackageForPath on the unmapped declaration-file path.

When saving, ReferenceType.toObject writes the numeric reflection id only if the target resolves inside the same project; otherwise it writes symbolId.toObject(), which keeps only package name, package path and qualified name (position and transient id are dropped). ProjectReflection.toObject also writes a symbolIdMap of its own reflections.

Application._convertPackages serializes each package project (serializer.projectToObject) and then calls Deserializer.reviveProjects, which revives each project as a module under one combined project. Each saved symbolIdMap is re-registered in a deferred step (de.defer) after oldIdToNewId is filled - in DeclarationReflection.fromObject for the project-variant branch used when merging, not in ProjectReflection.fromObject - and ReferenceType.fromObject rebuilds a ReflectionSymbolId and points the reference at the combined project.

CRITICAL: ProjectReflection keeps symbolToReflectionIdMap as a StableKeyMap keyed by ReflectionSymbolId.getStableKey(), which omits position and transient id when position is not finite (as for deserialized ids). A's deserialized reference and B's deserialized registration therefore share the key packageName/packagePath/qualifiedName, and the lazy ReferenceType.reflection getter resolves it through getReflectionsFromSymbolId, preferring type-like or value-like kinds according to preferValues.

On the page, formatter.tsx's reference handler uses type.reflection: when it resolves it renders each segment of getUniquePath as an anchor if router.hasUrl(item) (href from urlTo) and as a plain span otherwise; if it does not resolve it falls back to externalUrl or the bare name.

CRITICAL: BaseRouter.baseRelativeUrl counts the '/' characters in the current page's full URL (getFullUrl) and prefixes that many '../' to the target; for target './' with depth above zero it returns just the repeated '../' (avoiding '.././'), and at depth zero it yields './'.

The directory-style routers (KindDirRouter, StructureDirRouter) override getFullUrl (and relativeUrl) to strip the trailing 'index.html' through fixLink, so a page's URL ends in '/' and depth is counted on that directory form (e.g. 'classes/Foo/' gives '../../').

CRITICAL: The browser scripts (Search.ts state.base, Navigation.ts BASE_URL, Hierarchy.ts BASE_URL) read document.documentElement.dataset.base, append a trailing '/' if missing, and build every href as base + stored root-relative url.

Internationalization.setLocale merges the built-in table for that locale (de, en, fr, ja, ko, zh) with the user's overrides, falling back to the English table for a locale with no built-in text; addTranslations also updates the live table when it is for the loaded locale; Application warns that a language with no translations is unavailable and lists the supported ones (built-in plus any with user entries).

The i18n proxy in utils-common/i18n.ts looks up the message by key and substitutes {n} placeholders (the key itself is returned when it has no entry); translateTagName looks up 'tag_<name>' and otherwise builds an English title-cased name from the tag.

Tag and flag names: comment.tsx (block tag headings and modifier badges) and navigation.tsx (member-visibility filter labels) call translateTagName, and flag badges and filter labels use ReflectionFlags.flagString (flag_* keys).

probes.author: r3x-typedoc-drafter
probes.query: After the compiler-driven part of a run, several independent processing steps clean up and enrich the model: removing hidden members, merging modules on request, linking implementers and subclasses, copying inherited comments, grouping, categorising, resolving links, and so on. Give the order in which these steps run at the start and at the end of that stage, how that order is decided (including ties), and which of them run again when a project is restored from previously saved results instead, in what order, with what each repeated step does there. Say also which steps do not run again, and who triggers each of the two situations.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: Order is decided by listener priority: EventDispatcher.on uses insertPrioritySorted, so higher priority runs first and equal priorities keep registration order; registration order is the Converter constructor's plugin construction order (Category, Comment, Group, Implements, InheritDoc, LinkResolver, Package, Source, Type, Include, MergeModuleWith).

Start of the stage (Converter.resolve triggers resolve-begin, then one resolve event per reflection, then resolve-end): MergeModuleWithPlugin (priority 10000) first, then the priority-0 listeners in construction order: CommentPlugin (removes hidden reflections), PackagePlugin (project name/readme), SourcePlugin (source file names and links).

End of the stage: the priority-0 listeners ImplementsPlugin, InheritDocPlugin, TypePlugin (construction order), then GroupPlugin (-100), CategoryPlugin (-200) and LinkResolverPlugin (-300), so implementers and inherited comments exist before sections are built and links are resolved last.

CRITICAL: When a project is restored from saved results, Application triggers the revive event after Deserializer.reviveProjects (in _convertPackages and in _merge). Listeners run in this order: MergeModuleWithPlugin (10000), TypePlugin (100), then ImplementsPlugin, InheritDocPlugin, PackagePlugin (0), GroupPlugin (-100), CategoryPlugin (-200), LinkResolverPlugin (-300). CommentPlugin, SourcePlugin and IncludePlugin do not listen to it because their results were already serialized.

What repeats: MergeModuleWith merges tagged modules again; TypePlugin rebuilds implementedBy/extendedBy and the type hierarchy; ImplementsPlugin re-links implementations and inherited members; InheritDoc copies comments; PackagePlugin re-reads the manifest and readme for the project; GroupPlugin and CategoryPlugin rebuild sections only for the project and module/namespace reflections (not every container as at conversion); LinkResolverPlugin re-resolves links and external type links.

probes.author: r3x-typedoc-drafter
probes.query: My project has two entry modules which I listed in a deliberate order, one of which also has markdown documents attached, and nothing about ordering is configured. In what order do the modules appear in the sidebar and on the index page, in what order are the members of a class listed within its page, and in what order do the page's sections appear (give the English names of the first three sections on a module page that has documents, classes and functions)? Then explain what changes if the project is told to keep my order, what happens to a class's member order when a comment on that class names an ordering strategy with a misspelled word, and how a section that has no title is treated in the page and in the sidebar.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: The default strategy list is kind, instance-first, alphabetical-ignoring-documents (OptionDefaults.sort). getSortFunction builds a comparator that tries the strategies in turn and the first that distinguishes the two items decides; the kind strategy uses the user's kind order followed by any missing kinds in the default order (Document, Project, Module, Namespace, Enum, EnumMember, Class, Interface, TypeAlias, Constructor, Property, Variable, Function, Accessor, Method, Reference). Documents therefore come first and are never alphabetized, so they keep their original order.

Sections (groups) are not ordered by that comparator: GroupPlugin.sortGroupCallback orders them by weights, which by default are the plural kind names in a fixed order (Documents, Modules, Namespaces, ... - so a module page with documents, classes and functions shows Documents, Classes, Functions in that order); a group-order setting replaces the list and '*' marks where unlisted names go, otherwise unlisted names come last, ties broken alphabetically. When categories exist they are the sections instead (or are nested as 'group - category' when categorize-by-group is on) and are ordered by their own order setting with the same wildcard rule; CategoryPlugin re-sorts each category's children with the same comparator.

CRITICAL: GroupPlugin.group sorts a container's children, documents and combined list only when the keep-entry-order setting is on (default true) or none of its children is a module; so by default modules are sorted alphabetically by name, and when the setting is turned off a container whose children are modules keeps the order in which entry points (or modules) were created and its documents are left unsorted too.

A comment tag naming a strategy on the container replaces the default list for that container only. GroupPlugin.getSortFunction splits the text on commas/whitespace, warns for each invalid name and passes only the valid ones; CategoryPlugin silently drops invalid names. With a single misspelled name the list is empty, the comparator returns 0 for every pair, and the members stay in conversion (declaration) order.

A section titled 'none' (case-insensitive; the single section built when a container has children but no groups, or a group the user named so) is moved first by sortNoneSectionFirst in getMemberSections and rendered without a heading or collapsible wrapper in members.tsx/moduleReflection.tsx; in the sidebar, DefaultTheme.buildNavigation's filterMapWithNoneCollection lists its children first, directly, but only when sidebar grouping or categorising is switched on - by default the sidebar lists the already-sorted children flat.

probes.query: Documentation-coverage warnings are switched on. In my own package a class has a method with no comment at all. My package also re-exports a class that comes from a dependency installed as a third-party package and has no comments. A function elsewhere has a comment consisting of nothing but a visibility-style modifier. For which of these does the tool warn? Explain which kinds of item are checked by default and how functions, accessors and items nested inside a parameter or a type alias are handled, which package list is assumed when I give none and where that default comes from, what counts as 'has a comment', how to silence single items without turning the check off, and what the warning text tells me.
expectedFacts: The check runs only when the 'notDocumented' validation flag is on (default false in the validation option declaration); Application.validate then calls validateDocumentation with requiredToBeDocumented, intentionallyNotDocumented and the package list.

CRITICAL: By default Enum, EnumMember, Variable, Function, Class, Interface, Property, Method, Accessor and TypeAlias are required (not Constructor, Module, Namespace, parameters or type parameters). Functions/methods are checked through their call signatures, accessors through get/set signatures (constructors through constructor signatures if listed); selecting either Function or Method selects call signatures of both; a declaration that has signatures is skipped itself when it is a signature container. A signature counts as documented when its parent has a comment.

Indirections: anything with a Parameter ancestor is ignored; a type literal owned by a type alias, a call signature directly inside a type literal and a construct signature inside an alias are checked by checking the owning alias/declaration instead.

'Has a comment' is Reflection.hasComment -> Comment.hasVisibleComponent called without a not-rendered-tags list: any non-empty summary text, or any block tag at all, counts; a comment made only of modifier tags (such as a visibility modifier) does not, so that function is reported.

CRITICAL: Only reflections with a symbol id whose packageName is in packagesRequiringDocumentation are reported. When the user gave none, Application.validate uses [project.packageName ?? '<unknown>']; project.packageName is set by PackagePlugin.addEntries from the nearest valid package manifest found from the package directory (or the entry points' root). A symbol's package name comes from findPackageForPath in createSymbolIdImpl: the name after the last third-party-folder segment in its path (scoped-aware), otherwise the nearest manifest, so the re-exported dependency class is not reported unless its package is listed.

intentionallyNotDocumented entries are matched against Reflection.getFriendlyFullName() (for a signature, its parent's name); matched items are skipped, and entries that matched nothing produce a validation warning listing them. The reported text is '<name> (<kind>), defined in <package>/<path>, does not have any documentation', logged through validationWarning.

probes.query: A client span records the other side of the call it made: that side's service name and its network address. On the MySQL backend, follow that information from the moment spans are saved until a trace is fetched by its identifier and rebuilt into spans. Which stored rows carry the other side's network address, how does the key that marks them depend on the span's role, how is the address attached to the right span on read, and which separate column holds only the service name for searching?
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: On write, MySQLSpanConsumer.BatchInsertSpans.apply converts each v2 span to a v1 span with V2SpanConverter, and the remote endpoint is emitted as an address binary annotation whose key depends on the span kind: client 'sa', server 'ca', producer or consumer 'ma' ('sa' when a remote endpoint exists but the kind is unknown).
The address annotation is stored as a zipkin_annotations row with boolean type (0), a value of the single byte 1, and the endpoint columns filled from the remote endpoint, not the local one.

The remote service name is also written to zipkin_spans.remote_service_name, only when the schema has that column (null or 'unknown' become an empty string); this column serves search and name listing and is not used to rebuild the span's remote endpoint.

On read, SelectSpansAndAnnotations.apply loads span rows and annotation rows, and processAnnotationRecord accepts boolean-type rows only when the key is sa, ca or ma, the value is exactly one byte equal to 1, and an endpoint exists.

CRITICAL: V1SpanConverter.processBinaryAnnotations turns sa/ca/ma into the remoteEndpoint of the span that owns the matching core annotation endpoint (cs/cr for sa, sr/ss for ca, ms/mr for ma); with no core annotations a lone sa sets the remote endpoint on the first span, which has no kind.

On an old schema without the column, HasRemoteServiceName.test detects it (SQL state 42S22), so writes skip the column, getRemoteServiceNames returns an empty list, and a trace search filtered by remote service throws IllegalArgumentException.

probes.query: An operator of the Cassandra backend increases the setting for how many connections are kept to each database node. Follow that number from the server settings until it reaches the database driver. How many requests may each connection have outstanding afterwards, and what else does the code tell the driver when the session is built (read consistency, whether retries are safe, request timeout)? When is the session first created?
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: The operator setting travels ZipkinCassandra3StorageProperties.maxConnections (default 8) -> toBuilder().maxConnections(...) -> CassandraStorageBuilder.poolLocalSize (rejected if not positive).

CRITICAL: CassandraStorageBuilder.poolingOptions() returns two driver options, local pool size = poolLocalSize and max requests per connection = maxRequestsPerConnection; the latter is a final field initialised when the builder is created (40960 / 8 = 5120), so raising the connection count does not change the per-connection limit and total outstanding requests per node grow with the count.

CassandraStorage's constructor stores builder.poolingOptions(); DefaultSessionFactory.buildSession hands it to SessionBuilder.buildSession, which applies every entry with withInt on the programmatic driver configuration.

SessionBuilder.buildSession also sets request timeout to one minute, read consistency LOCAL_ONE, default idempotence true (all Zipkin CQL writes are idempotent), the local datacenter, and the SSL engine factory and hostname validation only when SSL is enabled.

The session is created lazily: LazySession.get calls sessionFactory.create(storage) the first time CassandraStorage.session() is needed (building the span consumer, span store or autocomplete store, or a health check); the factory is SessionFactory.DEFAULT exposed by ZipkinCassandra3StorageConfiguration.sessionFactory.

probes.query: On the Cassandra backend a span's local peer, remote peer and annotations are stored in structured column types, not as plain text. Follow how the database driver learns to convert those column values to and from the span model objects: where the converters are defined, when and on which object they are registered relative to schema installation and keyspace selection, what happens to the session if schema setup fails, and where a write and a read each rely on them.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: Writes and reads select the converters by Java type: InsertSpan.newCompletionStage binds l_ep and r_ep with Endpoint.class and annotations with Annotation.class, and SelectFromSpan.ReadSpans reads l_ep/r_ep with row.get(..., Endpoint.class) and annotations with getList(..., Annotation.class); the driver resolves the codec from its registry.

EndpointCodec and AnnotationCodec are MappingCodec subclasses wrapping the driver's UDT codec: EndpointCodec maps the UDT fields service, ipv4, ipv6 and port (null in, null out); AnnotationCodec maps field 0 (timestamp) and field 1 (value) and returns null when either is null.

CRITICAL: Schema.initializeUDTs reads the keyspace metadata, obtains the driver codecs for the 'annotation' and 'endpoint' user-defined types and registers the wrapped codecs in the session's MutableCodecRegistry.

Order in LazySession.get: sessionFactory.create, then ensureSchema (install or validate schema), then 'USE <keyspace>', then Schema.initializeUDTs, then preparing the health-check statement; component constructors (CassandraSpanConsumer, CassandraSpanStore) call storage.session() before preparing statements, so codecs exist first.

If ensureSchema or a later step throws RuntimeException or Error, LazySession closes the session without nulling it (so failed commands are not repeated) and get() throws ClosedComponentException ('Session initialization failed. See server logs') on that call; the codecs are not registered.

The UDTs are defined in zipkin2-schema.cql (endpoint: service, ipv4, ipv6, port; annotation: ts, v) with the default keyspace name replaced by Schema.applyCqlFile; InsertSpan skips null endpoints so no tombstones are written.

probes.query: Operators can relax the exact matching of trace identifiers, so that a 128-bit identifier and its lower 64-bit half count as the same trace. Across the shared storage helpers and all four storage implementations, name each place in production code where this relaxation changes what is written or how traces are looked up, group them by saving versus reading, and say what each does. Also say which helper filters results client-side when exact matching stays on.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: Elasticsearch changes the index mapping at template installation: VersionSpecificTemplates.spanIndexTemplate maps traceId as a plain keyword when matching is exact, but when relaxed it uses a text field with fielddata and a custom analyzer (pattern_capture on the trailing hex digits, original preserved); at read time ElasticsearchSpanStore.getTrace and getTraces cut a 32-character id to its lower 16 characters when relaxed, and getTraces(QueryRequest) adds StrictTraceId.filterTraces only when exact.

CRITICAL: Cassandra changes the stored layout when relaxed: InsertSpan.Factory.newInput splits a 32-character id into trace_id_high (first 16) and trace_id (last 16), and InsertTraceByServiceSpan and InsertTraceByServiceRemoteService index only the lower 16 characters; SelectFromSpan.Factory.newCall queries both the full and the lower id when relaxed and filters (StrictTraceId.filterSpans or filterTraces) when exact, and SelectSpansByTraceIds applies FilterTraces only when exact.

MySQL writing is unchanged (the high bits are stored whenever the schema has the column); on read SelectSpansAndAnnotations.Factory.create zeroes traceIdHigh when relaxed, Schema.spanTraceIdCondition and traceIdCondition compare (high, low) pairs only when the schema has the column and matching is exact, otherwise only the low half, and MySQLSpanStore adds StrictTraceId filters only when exact.

InMemoryStorage always indexes by the lower 64 bits (lowTraceId in doAccept); on read, when exact, getTrace, getTraces(QueryRequest) and getTraces(ids) regroup with strictByTraceId and keep only the exact ids, otherwise they return the merged low-64-bit trace.

Shared helpers: GroupByTraceId.map groups spans by the full trace id when exact and by the lower 16 characters when relaxed; StrictTraceId is the client-side filter used when exact (filterSpans drops spans whose trace id differs, filterTraces(ids) drops traces not in the id set, filterTraces(QueryRequest) re-filters only if two returned traces clash on the lower 64 bits).

The setting (default true) reaches each backend through its server configuration class (InMemoryConfiguration, ZipkinCassandra3StorageConfiguration, ZipkinMySQLStorageConfiguration, ZipkinElasticsearchStorageConfiguration).

probes.query: An operator gives the Elasticsearch storage one setting that lists several addresses: some bare host names, one with a secure scheme, one with the old native-transport port, one without a port. InitialEndpointSupplier.get splits on commas (empty pieces skipped); an entry with http:// or https:// is parsed as a URI; a bare host without a colon gets ':9200' appended only when the protocol is not TLS; otherwise the protocol scheme is prefixed to the entry; blank or null hosts become '<protocol>://localhost:9200'.

An IP literal or 'localhost' becomes a fixed Endpoint, any other host name becomes a DnsAddressEndpointGroup that round-robins over all resolved addresses, and all are combined into one EndpointGroup.

MultiplexingMiddleware.MapAsync asks the factory for the aggregator only after all sub-calls have already run, so a missing name is detected after the backend calls were made.
UserDefinedResponseAggregator.Aggregate puts the provider error (CouldNotFindAggregatorError) on the original context errors instead of producing a response.
CRITICAL: ErrorsToHttpStatusCodeMapper has no branch for that error code, so ResponderMiddleware sets 404 through the final default return; the 404 stored inside the error object is never consulted.

probes.query: An operator submits a complete replacement settings document to the gateway's runtime administration interface, and the document fails validation. Follow it: which handler receives it, which service applies it, in what order that service touches the stored settings files versus the live in-memory configuration, where validation runs, which exception carries the failure, and what text shape the operator gets back. CRITICAL: FileAndInternalConfigurationSetter.SetAsync first persists through IFileConfigurationRepository.SetAsync and only afterwards builds the internal configuration; if creation reports errors it throws ConfigurationRepositoryException and never calls AddOrReplace.

CRITICAL: DiskFileConfigurationRepository.SetAsync deletes and rewrites the environment-specific file and then the primary ocelot.json, then activates the change-token source, all before validation; so the invalid document stays on disk and the signal is raised once, while the live in-memory configuration stays unchanged.

Validation runs inside FileInternalConfigurationCreator.Create via IConfigurationValidator.IsValid (FileConfigurationFluentValidator), whose failures become FileValidationFailedError items; ConfigurationRepositoryException builds its message by joining the errors as "Code: Message" lines.

On success InMemoryInternalConfigurationRepository.AddOrReplace replaces the stored configuration under a lock and activates the change-token source again, so a successful upload raises the signal twice; OcelotConfigurationChangeToken.HasChanged stays true for one second.

Each ordinary call reads the current configuration: ConfigurationMiddleware, the first middleware in the Ocelot pipeline, calls IInternalConfigurationRepository.Get and stores it on HttpContext.Items.

probes.query: An operator turns on the per-route switch that asks the gateway to trace its backend calls. Follow it end to end. (1) Where is it decided that the switch has any effect, and what happens if the host application never supplied a tracing component? (2) Where is the tracing wrapper added to the outgoing handler chain, and where is it built? (3) Through which callback does the tracing component hand an identifier back, and where does that identifier get stored for the current call? (4) The operator then adds a custom header whose value is the placeholder for that identifier, once to the request sent to the backend and once to the reply sent to the caller. Which of the two can carry the identifier, why, and what happens to a header of the same name that the client already sent in the failing case?
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: HttpHandlerOptionsCreator reads an optional IOcelotTracer from the service provider, and the effective UseTracing is true only when a tracer is registered and the route/global flag is true (Merge: `_tracer != null && options.UseTracing.Value`; other branches via HttpHandlerOptions(from, useTracing)); with no tracer the flag silently has no effect and no error is raised.

DelegatingHandlerFactory.Get appends the handler from ITracingHandlerFactory.Get when route.HttpHandlerOptions.UseTracing is true, after user handlers and before the QoS handler; TracingHandlerFactory.Get builds OcelotHttpTracingHandler(tracer, repo).

OcelotHttpTracingHandler.SendAsync calls IOcelotTracer.SendAsync passing its AddTraceId method as the callback together with base.SendAsync; AddTraceId stores the id through IRequestScopedDataRepository.Add under the TraceId key, and HttpDataRepository.Add puts it in HttpContext.Items.
CRITICAL: Placeholders resolves the trace-id placeholder lazily with GetTraceId, reading that stored value; when no value exists it yields CouldNotFindPlaceholderError.

HttpHeadersTransformationMiddleware applies the request-side added headers before calling the rest of the pipeline (before the tracing handler runs, so no id exists) and applies the reply-side added headers after it returns, only when there are no pipeline errors; so only the reply-side header can carry the identifier.

AddHeadersToRequest removes any existing header with the same name before resolving the placeholder, and when the lookup fails it logs a warning and skips adding it, so a header the client sent with that name is lost.

probes.query: When a new configuration replaces the running one, which of the gateway's own in-memory tables, used for choosing a route or backend, remembering balancer progress or sending the call, keep their old entries? LoadBalancerHouse._loadBalancers is keyed by route.LoadBalancerKey and reuses an entry when the key and balancer type match, so entries survive a configuration swap.
RoundRobin.LastIndices is a static dictionary keyed by the service name (route ServiceName, else LoadBalancerKey), so it is process-wide and untouched by a swap.
CookieStickySessions.Stored is a static dictionary keyed "LoadBalancerKey:cookie value"; entries leave only through the expiry check scheduled on its bus, never on configuration swap.

DiscoveryDownstreamRouteFinder._cache memoises the route holder by load balancer key from the first call onward and is never invalidated, so it can keep serving options from the earlier configuration.

CRITICAL: A swap is only InMemoryInternalConfigurationRepository.AddOrReplace replacing one field and activating the change-token source; nothing in src subscribes to that signal, so nothing clears these tables.

probes.query: A route does not state which HTTP protocol version or version policy the backend call should use, while the global section does. Which values does the backend call end up with in each of three cases: an ordinary fixed-address route, a route entry meant for discovery-based services, and a call matched to no route entry at all but routed purely by discovery? DynamicRoutesCreator uses the route text IfEmpty the global text for both the version and the policy before calling the creators.

CRITICAL: For a call with no dynamic route entry, DiscoveryDownstreamRouteFinder.Get builds the route from the internal configuration global values created by ConfigurationCreator.Create; when a matching dynamic entry exists, its already-resolved values replace them.
HttpVersionCreator silently returns 1.1 on parse failure; HttpVersionPolicyCreator maps the three known policy names and returns RequestVersionOrLower for anything else.

Only the ordinary route text is validated at start-up (RouteFluentValidator: version pattern with one digit and optional one-digit fraction, policy one of the three names); global and dynamic-entry texts are not validated, and a bare major number matches the pattern yet Version.TryParse needs major.minor, so it also ends as 1.1.
RequestMapper.Map copies the DownstreamRoute version and policy onto the HttpRequestMessage Version and VersionPolicy.
