probes.query: Routes can carry free-form key/value text entries that custom handlers read back later, and the global section can carry such entries too. Which entry wins when both define the same key, which section decides how the text is split into a list, parsed as a number or read as yes/no (and can one route change that), what does a reader get for a missing key or an unrecognised yes/no word, and for a call matched to no route entry but routed purely by discovery, which entries are visible?
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: DefaultMetadataCreator.Create copies the global entries into a new dictionary and then overwrites them with the route entries, so the route value wins for the same key.

CRITICAL: Separators, trim characters, split option, number style and culture come only from the global file options (defaults: comma separator, space trim char, no split option, Any number style, current culture); a route cannot override them.

DownstreamRouteExtensions.GetMetadata returns the caller default when there are no entries, the key is missing or its value is null; strings come back as is, lists are split by the separators, trimmed and stripped of empty items, numbers are parsed with the configured style and culture, other types are JSON-deserialized.

For bool, only the words true, yes, on, ok, enable, enabled and 1 (trimmed, case-insensitive) give true and everything else gives false; for a nullable bool true words give true, false words (false, no, off, disable, disabled, 0) give false, and any other word gives null.

For a call with no matching route entry, DiscoveryDownstreamRouteFinder.Get uses configuration.MetadataOptions that ConfigurationCreator.Create built from the global entries only (route entries null); when a dynamic route entry matches, it uses that entry merged options.

probes.query: Application code receives a response but never closes it, and the call object is later reclaimed by the garbage collector. Explain what notices this and when that check runs, what it does to the connection that call was using, how the place where the call began can be captured and reported, and how the reporting differs on a server JVM, on an Android 11 or newer device, and on an older Android device. Name the file and component for each step.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: Detection is in RealConnectionPool.pruneAndGetAllocationCount, called for every connection from closeConnections (the pool's cleanup task). Each connection keeps a list of RealCall.CallReference objects (weak references to the call); a reference whose get() is null means the call was garbage collected without finishing, so the pool reports it through Platform.get().logCloseableLeak(message, callReference.callStackTrace), removes the reference, and if no calls remain sets the connection's idleAtNs to now minus the keep-alive duration so it is evicted at once.

The creation site is captured in RealCall.callStart with Platform.get().getStackTraceForCloseable(...), stored in RealCall.callStackTrace, and copied into the CallReference by RealCall.acquireConnectionNoEvents when the call takes a connection.

CRITICAL: On a server JVM (base Platform) getStackTraceForCloseable returns a Throwable only if the OkHttpClient java.util.logging logger is loggable at FINE and otherwise null; logCloseableLeak then appends a hint to raise that logger to FINE when the trace is null and logs at WARN through Platform.log.

On Android 11+ (Android10Platform, SDK_INT >= 30) the captured object is an android.util.CloseGuard opened with the closer text and logCloseableLeak calls CloseGuard.warnIfOpen(); below SDK 30 (Android 10 itself and the older AndroidPlatform for API 21-28, which overrides neither function) the base Platform behaviour is used, and log is overridden to Log.w/Log.i with tag OkHttp.

On Android the FINE check depends on AndroidLog.enable(), called from PlatformRegistry.findPlatform: it maps the OkHttpClient logger to tag okhttp.OkHttpClient and sets its level to FINE only if Log.isLoggable(tag, DEBUG) at startup, so the stack trace exists on older Android only when that tag has debug logging enabled.

The check only runs when closeConnections runs: it is scheduled by scheduleCloser (on pool put and when a connection becomes idle), and closeConnections returns the keep-alive duration (default 5 minutes from the ConnectionPool defaults) while connections are in use, and -1 when the pool is empty; the Task.runOnce return value is the next delay and TaskRunner.afterRun reschedules unless it is -1.

probes.query: A server's cookie names a domain that is broader than the page host and is a registry-controlled suffix such as a country-code zone. Where does the client refuse it, which data does that decision consult, where does that data physically come from on a server JVM versus an Android app, and what must have happened in an Android app before the first such decision can succeed? Also say what a second thread sees while the first one is still loading the data, and what happens if loading fails. Name the file and component for each step.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: Cookie parsing (Cookie.kt around lines 559-567) first requires the cookie domain to domain-match the URL host; if the domain is shorter than the host (not host-only) and PublicSuffixDatabase.get().getEffectiveTldPlusOne(domain) is null (the domain is itself a public suffix), the Set-Cookie is rejected (parse returns null).

PublicSuffixDatabase.getEffectiveTldPlusOne calls findMatchingRule, which first calls publicSuffixList.ensureLoaded(); the singleton instance is created as PublicSuffixDatabase(PublicSuffixList.Default), where Default is an expect val with one actual per source set.

CRITICAL: On a server JVM the actual Default (jvmMain PublicSuffixList.jvm.kt) is ResourcePublicSuffixList, reading the classpath resource okhttp3/internal/publicsuffix/PublicSuffixDatabase.list through FileSystem.RESOURCES; on Android the actual (androidMain PublicSuffixList.android.kt) is AssetPublicSuffixList, reading the asset PublicSuffixDatabase.list through PlatformRegistry.applicationContext?.assets (the file exists as androidMain/assets/PublicSuffixDatabase.list and jvmMain/resources/okhttp3/internal/publicsuffix/PublicSuffixDatabase.list).

On Android the application context is held by the platform object (AndroidPlatform or Android10Platform, both ContextAwarePlatform) through PlatformRegistry.applicationContext; it is set by the AndroidX Startup initializer PlatformInitializer (registered as meta-data in androidMain/AndroidManifest.xml) or by OkHttp.initialize(context), which only assigns when still null and uses the application context; without it AssetPublicSuffixList throws an IOException (message differs when Build.FINGERPRINT is null, a unit test without Robolectric).

BasePublicSuffixList.ensureLoaded lets the first caller win an AtomicBoolean compareAndSet and read the file (two length-prefixed byte blocks: the rule list and the exception list); other threads block on a CountDownLatch until the read completes.

If reading fails with an IOException, BasePublicSuffixList stores it as readFailure and ensureLoaded then throws IllegalStateException('Unable to load <path> resource.') with that cause, so cookie parsing fails with that exception rather than silently accepting.

probes.query: A server speaking the multiplexed protocol tells the client it is going away and names the last stream it processed. Trace what happens to the requests already in flight on that connection, what exception the application thread ends up with and where it is produced, how the connection's failure counters change, and how later calls are kept off that connection. Also say what happens to a call that tries to open a new stream just after the notice. Name the file and component for each step.
expectedFacts: Http2Reader.readGoAway validates the frame (length at least 8, stream id 0, a known error code) and hands lastStreamId, error code and debug data to the handler's goAway.

CRITICAL: Http2Connection.ReaderRunnable.goAway sets isShutdown = true and, for every stream with id greater than lastGoodStreamId that was initiated locally, calls Http2Stream.receiveRstStream(REFUSED_STREAM) and removeStream; streams with ids up to the named last stream are left running.

Http2Stream.receiveRstStream stores the error code and wakes waiters, so Http2Stream.takeHeaders (called by Http2ExchangeCodec.readResponseHeaders) or the body source read throws a StreamResetException carrying REFUSED_STREAM; Exchange.readResponseHeaders catches the IOException, calls trackFailure and rethrows.

Exchange.trackFailure calls codec.carrier.trackFailure, which is RealConnection.trackFailure: a StreamResetException with REFUSED_STREAM only increments refusedStreamCount, and only from the second one does it set noNewExchanges and increment routeFailureCount.

CRITICAL: Later calls are kept off the connection by health, not by those counters: Http2Connection.isHealthy returns false once isShutdown, so RealConnectionPool.callAcquirePooledConnection (after acquiring an eligible connection) and RealRoutePlanner.planReuseCallConnection mark it noNewExchanges, release it and close the socket if it is idle.

A call that races and opens a stream after the notice gets ConnectionShutdownException from Http2Connection.newStream (isShutdown); RealConnection.trackFailure treats it as noNewExchanges plus, if the connection has no successful call yet, connectFailed for the route and routeFailureCount++, and RetryAndFollowUpInterceptor.recover treats it as 'request not sent' (requestSendStarted false).

probes.query: A server tries to push an unrequested resource to the client over the multiplexed protocol. Trace what the client does from the moment the promise arrives: who is asked, what the default answer is and what the client sends back, and what happens to frames that later arrive for the promised stream. Also name the places that look as if they handle server-initiated streams or the client's push preference but do not apply to this case.
expectedFacts: Http2Reader.readPushPromise rejects stream id 0, reads the promised stream id and decodes the header block, then calls handler.pushPromise, which Http2Connection.ReaderRunnable.pushPromise forwards to pushRequestLater(promisedStreamId, headers).

CRITICAL: pushRequestLater answers PROTOCOL_ERROR (writeSynResetLater) if the promised id is already in currentPushRequests; otherwise it records the id and runs pushObserver.onRequest on the pushQueue task queue, and when that returns true (cancel) it writes RST_STREAM with ErrorCode.CANCEL and forgets the id.

CRITICAL: The observer on a client connection is the Http2Connection.Builder default PushObserver.CANCEL (nothing in RealConnection.startHttp2 or elsewhere in production code sets another): onRequest and onHeaders return true, onData skips the bytes and returns true, onReset does nothing.

Frames for pushed (even-numbered, nonzero) stream ids never reach the normal stream map: ReaderRunnable.data, headers and rstStream check pushedStream(streamId) first and call pushDataLater (reads the frame eagerly), pushHeadersLater and pushResetLater, each delegating to the observer and cancelling again.

Decoy: RealConnection.onStream (closes remotely initiated streams with REFUSED_STREAM) is the Http2Connection.Listener hook for peer-created streams, but the reader's pushedStream check routes even ids before listener.onStream is reachable for a client.

Decoy: Settings.getEnablePush is marked TODO (not honoured) and unused; the client's own SETTINGS (okHttpSettings) only set the 16 MiB initial window size and do not disable push; Http2Reader.readSettings only validates that a received ENABLE_PUSH value is 0 or 1.

probes.query: List every place along an ordinary request path where a time limit is armed, applied, or reset (leave out web sockets and the periodic liveness probe), and say which configured value feeds each one. Include how a fresh connection differs from a reused one, and how the two protocol versions differ.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: The whole-call limit is RealCall.timeout, an AsyncTimeout set to client.callTimeoutMillis; it is entered in RealCall.execute and in AsyncCall.run, its timedOut cancels the call, and timeoutExit turns a fired timeout into InterruptedIOException('timeout'); upgrades and duplex calls stop it early through timeoutEarlyExit.

RealInterceptorChain holds the per-call connect, read and write values (initialised from the client, replaced through withConnectTimeout, withReadTimeout and withWriteTimeout, only before an exchange exists); RealCall.enterNetworkInterceptorExchange feeds them into RealRoutePlanner: connect becomes socketConnectTimeoutMillis, read becomes both readTimeoutMillis and socketReadTimeoutMillis, write becomes writeTimeoutMillis.

CRITICAL: For a fresh connection, ConnectPlan.connectSocket sets rawSocket.soTimeout to socketReadTimeoutMillis and calls Platform.connectSocket with socketConnectTimeoutMillis, so the read value also bounds reads during the TLS handshake; ConnectPlan.createTunnel sets the proxy CONNECT source and sink timeouts from readTimeoutMillis and writeTimeoutMillis.

RealConnection.newCodec runs for every exchange: for HTTP/1 it sets the socket soTimeout and the buffered source and sink timeouts to the current call's read and write values (so a reused connection adopts the new call's limits), and Http1ExchangeCodec.detachTimeout clears the per-exchange ForwardingTimeout when request or response bodies finish so limits are not shared between pooled uses.

For HTTP/2, RealConnection.startHttp2 sets the socket soTimeout to 0 because limits are per stream; Http2ExchangeCodec.writeRequestHeaders sets the stream's read and write timeouts from the chain values.
Http2Stream.doReadTimeout means a client stream enforces its read timeout only once the request body sink is closed or finished (matters for duplex calls).

probes.query: On Android, the client may meet several different kinds of TLS socket: the one built into the operating system, one from a security-provider update delivered by Google's services, two from optional third-party security libraries, and one that exists only on the very newest OS release. For each kind, which component recognises it, what makes that component usable at all, and how does it switch on application-protocol negotiation? Also say which components are consulted on OS releases before Android 10, and which one is the only kind that can extract the trust manager from a custom socket factory.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: AndroidPlatform (API 21-28) builds its adapter list as StandardAndroidSocketAdapter.buildIfSupported(), DeferredSocketAdapter(AndroidSocketAdapter.playProviderFactory), DeferredSocketAdapter(ConscryptSocketAdapter.factory), DeferredSocketAdapter(BouncyCastleSocketAdapter.factory), filtered by isSupported(); Android10Platform (API 29+) instead starts with Android17SocketAdapter.buildIfSupported() and Android10SocketAdapter.buildIfSupported() followed by the same three deferred adapters; configureTlsExtensions and getSelectedProtocol use the first adapter whose matchesSocket is true, and with none (a custom socket class) no extension is configured.

The OS-built-in socket before Android 10 is recognised by StandardAndroidSocketAdapter (reflection on com.android.org.conscrypt OpenSSLSocketImpl, OpenSSLSocketFactoryImpl and SSLParametersImpl; it logs 'unable to load android socket classes' and yields null if the classes are missing) and configured by reflection in AndroidSocketAdapter (setUseSessionTickets, setAlpnProtocols with length-prefixed bytes, setHostname only on SDK 23 and below, getAlpnSelectedProtocol).

CRITICAL: The Google-services provider socket is matched purely by class-name prefix com.google.android.gms.org.conscrypt. through AndroidSocketAdapter.playProviderFactory (a DeferredSocketAdapter factory), then handled by the same reflective AndroidSocketAdapter, found by walking superclasses to OpenSSLSocketImpl; DeferredSocketAdapter creates its delegate lazily on the first matching socket and always reports isSupported true.

Android10SocketAdapter (usable when SDK_INT >= 29) matches sockets with SSLSockets.isSupportedSocket and configures session tickets plus SSLParameters.applicationProtocols using Platform.alpnProtocolNames; Android17SocketAdapter (usable when SDK_INT >= 37) does the same and additionally applies a parsed ECH config list, skipping an unparsable one.

ConscryptSocketAdapter is usable only if org.conscrypt classes load and Conscrypt.isAvailable() with version at least 2.1.0, matches with Conscrypt.isConscrypt(sslSocket), and sets session tickets and application protocols through Conscrypt; BouncyCastleSocketAdapter is usable only if org.bouncycastle.jsse.provider.BouncyCastleJsseProvider loads, matches sockets that are BCSSLSocket, and sets SSLParameters.applicationProtocols.

Only StandardAndroidSocketAdapter overrides matchesSocketFactory and trustManager (reflecting the sslParameters field and its x509TrustManager or trustManager field); the other adapters inherit the interface defaults (false and null), so AndroidPlatform.trustManager/Android10Platform.trustManager return null for any other factory.

probes.query: The DNS-over-HTTPS resolver keeps its own cache of answers, separate from the application's HTTP response cache. How long is an answer served, when does it get refreshed, how are failures and empty answers cached, and which record types share entries? Also say what bounds the number of entries and what decides which ones are evicted, and whether the operating system's default resolver goes through this cache. Name the file and component for each rule.
expectedFacts: The public DnsCache defaults are minimum TTL 10 s, maximum TTL 300 s, failure TTL 10 s, revalidate-before-expire 2 s and 1000 entries; it wraps a RealDnsCache and is used only by DnsOverHttps (Builder default DnsCache(); queryFactory = cache.-delegate.wrap(DnsOverHttpsQuery.Factory)); the default system resolver (Dns.SYSTEM, InetAddressDns) never goes through it.

CRITICAL: Entries are keyed by the DNS Question (name, type, class), so A, AAAA and HTTPS (service metadata) answers are cached separately; DnsOverHttps.newCall builds StateMachineDnsCall, which asks HTTPS (when includeServiceMetadata, with the _port._https. name for a non-443 port), AAAA (when includeIPv6) and A, while DnsOverHttps.lookup runs a copy with includeServiceMetadata = false that shares the same cache.

CRITICAL: RealDnsCache.CacheQuery.onResponse sets the lifetime to the minimum answer TTL (seconds) coerced into [minimumTimeToLive, maximumTimeToLive], or to failureTimeToLive when the response has no answers; revalidateAt = sentAt + max(0, lifetime - revalidateBeforeExpire) and expireAt = sentAt + lifetime. onFailure stores a Failure result for failureTimeToLive and replays that exception to queries until it expires.

CacheQuery.enqueue serves the stored result while now < expireAt, and starts a new network query when there is no result or now >= revalidateAt (so within the last revalidate window a still-valid answer is returned immediately while a refresh runs in the background); if the result is expired and a query is already in flight, the caller joins that in-flight call; cancelling a CacheQuery does not cancel the network query, so the cache is still updated.

MemoryCache.computeIfAbsent never evicts until the entry count reaches twice maxSize and then evicts down to maxSize in one batch (maxSize 0 disables caching: a new Entry each time and nothing stored); RealDnsCache.lastRequestedAt returns null for entries that are expired with no in-flight call (evicted unconditionally) and otherwise the last request time, and MemoryCache.evict removes the least recently requested using a priority queue that drops the newest.

probes.query: A client uses the default trust settings and has no certificate-fingerprint pins for the host it connects to. Does the library rebuild or tidy the presented certificate chain while it sets up the connection? Say where and when that tidying actually runs, how the component that does it is chosen on a server JVM versus on Android, what the tidied chain looks like, and what happens if the tidying fails. Name the file and component for each rule.
expectedFacts: OkHttpClient's init block, when the builder has no custom socket factory, takes Platform.get().platformTrustManager(), builds certificateChainCleaner = CertificateChainCleaner.get(trustManager) (which calls Platform.buildCertificateChainCleaner) and gives it to the pinner with withCertificateChainCleaner; with a custom factory the cleaner is computed in the Builder (from the supplied trust manager, or through Platform.trustManager for the legacy overload).

CRITICAL: The cleaner is chosen by Platform.buildCertificateChainCleaner: the base implementation is BasicCertificateChainCleaner over a BasicTrustRootIndex of the trust manager's accepted issuers; AndroidPlatform and Android10Platform override it to AndroidCertificateChainCleaner.buildIfSupported(trustManager) (which needs X509TrustManagerExtensions, i.e. a trust manager with the host-aware checkServerTrusted) and fall back to the base one when null.

CRITICAL: ConnectPlan.connectTls does not clean the chain eagerly: after the hostname verifier passes it builds the Handshake with a lambda that calls certificatePinner.certificateChainCleaner.clean(peerCertificates, host), then calls certificatePinner.check(host) { handshake.peerCertificates }; CertificatePinner.check calls findMatchingPins first and returns immediately when no pin matches the host, so the lambda never runs.
Handshake.peerCertificates is a lazy property over that provider: the cleaning runs on the first read, and a SSLPeerUnverifiedException thrown by it is swallowed, giving an empty list.

Readers that force it include RealConnection.isEligible for coalescing onto a different host (supportsUrl reads handshake.peerCertificates for the hostname check and the pinner check receives handshake().peerCertificates as an argument) and application code that reads Response.handshake().peerCertificates.

BasicCertificateChainCleaner.clean starts from the leaf, follows issuers (at most MAX_SIGNERS = 9) from the presented chain, appends the trusted anchor found via the TrustRootIndex unless it is already last, and throws SSLPeerUnverifiedException when no trusted certificate signed the chain or it is too long; the Android cleaner returns X509TrustManagerExtensions.checkServerTrusted(chain, 'RSA', host) and converts CertificateException into SSLPeerUnverifiedException.

probes.query: With the PostgreSQL adapter that wraps the native C client library and default connection options, a query returns rows that have a date column, a time-of-day column and a timestamp-with-zone column. Starting when the result set arrives, trace how each column's raw text becomes a Ruby value: which code chooses a converter for each column from its server-side type number, where the table of converters is first filled and then adjusted when the database object is created, what makes the date converter safe to be so simple, and which code applies the database-side and application-side time zone settings to the timestamp.
expectedFacts: Postgres::Dataset#fetch_rows_set_cols (adapters/postgres.rb) looks up each result field's type number (res.ftype) in db.conversion_procs and builds [converter, column symbol] pairs; yield_hash_rows calls the converter on every non-nil value.

The converter table starts as the shared CONVERSION_PROCS constant (adapters/shared/postgres.rb): type 1082 (date) maps to a date translator, 1083/1266 (time) to Sequel.string_to_time, and 1114/1184 (timestamp, timestamptz) to Sequel.database_to_application_timestamp; each Database duplicates it in initialize_postgres_adapter.

CRITICAL: initialize_postgres_adapter then replaces the 1114 and 1184 entries with the Database instance's own to_application_timestamp method, so timestamp conversion is per database object (honouring its timezone setting) rather than the global default converter.

CRITICAL: Postgres::Database#adapter_initialize replaces the date entry (1082) with TYPE_TRANSLATOR_DATE, which only splits the text on '-' and builds Date.new, unless the use_iso_date_format option is false (default true).
The simple date converter is safe because the same option makes connection_configuration_sqls add the session statement that sets the date output style to ISO on every new connection.

Database#to_application_timestamp (database/misc.rb) calls Sequel.convert_timestamp(v, timezone) with the Database's timezone (falling back to Sequel.database_timezone); convert_timestamp (timezones.rb) parses the text, uses the database timezone only when the text has no explicit UTC offset, then converts the result to Sequel.application_timezone.

probes.query: A model has a one-to-many relationship. Application code passes the parent a list of attribute hashes through the generated bulk-assignment setter for that relationship: one hash describes a brand-new child, another matches an existing child by primary key and carries a delete marker, and the configuration for that relationship allows deletion. Nothing has been saved yet. Explain what happens until the parent is saved: how the setter routes each hash, how validation of the new child is postponed and how its errors reach the parent, which mechanism postpones the database work until after the parent's own write and where that mechanism empties itself, which method finally attaches the new child and what it sets on it, and why the child marked for deletion is not first detached from the parent.
expectedFacts: The generated '<association>_attributes=' setter (defined by nested_attributes/def_nested_attribute_method) calls set_nested_attributes, which for an array association calls nested_attributes_list_setter and then nested_attributes_setter per hash: a hash whose primary key matches an existing child with the delete flag (allowed by the destroy option) goes to nested_attributes_remove(destroy: true); a hash with no matching key goes to nested_attributes_create.

nested_attributes_create builds the child with set/set_fields, registers delay_validate_associated_object, appends the child to the cached association array, marks it skip_validation_on_next_save!, and registers an after_save hook that calls the reflection's add_ method.

validate_associated's delay_validate_associated_object registers an after_validation hook; validate_associated_object fills the child's foreign key from the parent's primary key when missing, validates the child, and copies the child's error messages onto the parent's errors under the association name (ignoring foreign-key errors if the parent has no key yet).

CRITICAL: the postponing mechanism is the instance_hooks plugin: after_save_hook/after_validation_hook store blocks in @instance_hooks, the overridden after_save runs the after_save hooks after the parent's save and then deletes the :after_save, :before_save, :after_validation and :before_validation entries.

CRITICAL: the add_ method is add_associated_object (associations.rb), which runs the private _add_ method built from the one_to_many :adder proc; that proc sets the child's foreign key column(s) from the parent's key and saves the child.

For the doomed child nested_attributes_remove only detaches (remove_ method) when destroy is not requested or reflection.remove_before_destroy? is true; OneToManyAssociationReflection#remove_before_destroy? is false, so it only registers an after_save hook calling obj.destroy and deletes the child from the cached association array.

probes.query: On PostgreSQL, a model's table has a 32-bit integer column, a decimal column with declared precision and scale, and a timestamp column. The developer turns on the model feature that derives validations automatically from the table definition. Explain where the lower and upper bounds that a too-large integer or a far-future date is compared against come from: which code computes them and from what text, when and where the results are cached, how they reach the model's validation step, under which conditions the bound check is skipped, and why a model on the embedded single-file database gets no integer bounds at all.
expectedFacts: setup_auto_validations (auto_validations.rb) builds auto_validate_max_value_columns and auto_validate_min_value_columns from every db_schema entry that has :max_value / :min_value; it runs when the plugin is configured and again after every set_dataset (Plugins.after_set_dataset).

The bounds are checked in the plugin's validate method, only inside the schema-types branch (skipped if types validation is skipped or disabled), by validates_max_value / validates_min_value with options that allow nil and skip a column that already has an error (e.g. a type error).

CRITICAL: the db_schema comes from Model.get_db_schema -> Database#schema (database/query.rb), which caches parsed results in @schemas (when cache_schema is true) and, after schema_parse_table, fills :min_value/:max_value for columns that lack both: integer columns via column_schema_integer_min_max_values, decimal columns via column_schema_decimal_min_max_values.

The integer guess reads the db_type text: names containing big/int8 give the 64-bit range, small/int2 the 16-bit range, otherwise the 32-bit range (unsigned variants for MySQL-style 'unsigned'); the decimal guess uses the declared precision and scale (from :column_size/:scale or the '(p,s)' in db_type) as plus or minus the largest representable value.

CRITICAL: for PostgreSQL date and timestamp columns the bounds are set earlier, inside Postgres schema_parse_table (server 9.6+): date type 1082 gets MIN_DATE/MAX_DATE and timestamp types 1114/1184 get MIN_TIMESTAMP/MAX_TIMESTAMP only when Sequel.datetime_class is Time; query.rb's guard (skip if :max_value or :min_value already set) leaves them unchanged.

The SQLite adapter overrides column_schema_integer_min_max_values to return nil (decimal is an alias of it), because SQLite does not restrict integer or decimal columns to a range, so no bounds are stored and no bound validation is added.

probes.query: A model hierarchy keeps each subclass's extra columns in a separate table linked to the parent table by primary key, and the parent table has a type column that names the subclass of each row. Application code loads all rows of the parent model with the call that returns a list, then reads a subclass-only attribute on the first returned object. probes.query: When a model instance is saved on PostgreSQL or on SQLite, its in-memory column values may be refreshed with values the database computed (defaults, generated keys, trigger changes). Which places in the library decide where those values come from for a newly created row or an updated row: in the same statement, in a follow-up read, or not at all? Cover the core model save logic, the capability checks on the query-object side for each of the two databases and their default, and every optional add-on that changes this for creates or updates. Name each place and what it decides.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: Model::InstanceMethods#_insert uses _use_insert_select?(ds) (true when the dataset has no custom select or already has :returning, and ds.supports_insert_select?) to run one INSERT ... RETURNING via _insert_select_raw and set all values; otherwise it runs a plain insert and returns the primary key.

In _save, when _insert returned a primary key, _save_refresh does a follow-up read (_refresh_get, using the fast primary-key SQL when available) and replaces @values; when insert_select already filled the values _insert returns nil and no follow-up read happens.

Dataset#supports_insert_select? defaults to supports_returning?(:insert), which is false by default (dataset/features.rb); PostgreSQL overrides supports_insert_select? to be true unless the dataset was marked disable_insert_returning, and supports_returning? is true (merge needs 17+).

CRITICAL: on SQLite supports_returning? is true only for SQLite 3.35.0 or newer (db.sqlite_version >= 33500), so older SQLite falls back to insert plus follow-up SELECT; PostgreSQL and SQLite insert_select append RETURNING and fetch the first row (returning false if no row).

plugins/insert_returning_select makes models whose dataset has a custom select list use an insert dataset with a RETURNING clause limited to those columns (instance_insert_dataset), re-enabling single-statement refresh for them; plugins/skip_create_refresh turns _save_refresh into a no-op.

plugins/update_refresh overrides _update_without_checking to use UPDATE ... RETURNING (merging the returned row into @values) when supports_returning?(:update), and otherwise refreshes in after_update.

probes.query: On PostgreSQL, a table-creation block declares an auto-generated primary key column named id without giving a type. Which SQL text results for that column on a recent server and on an old server (before version 10.2), and what decides between the two? What changes when the block asks for a 64-bit type, and when the column also receives an explicit default value? After the table exists, how does schema inspection decide the key is auto-generated? Name every place whose logic affects the final column text.
expectedFacts: CreateTableGenerator#primary_key merges @db.serial_primary_key_options with the column name (and any type/options argument); on PostgreSQL that hash is {primary_key: true, identity: true, type: Integer} when server_version >= 100002, otherwise {primary_key: true, serial: true, type: Integer} (the generic Database default with :auto_increment is a decoy).
server_version (shared/postgres.rb) queries current_setting('server_version_num') once and memoizes it (0 if the query fails, which selects the serial branch).

CRITICAL: on a recent server the column text is the quoted name, 'integer' (type_literal_generic_integer returns :serial only when column[:serial]), then ' GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY' (added by Postgres column_definition_default_sql because the type is not a serial type and no :default exists), then ' PRIMARY KEY'; on an old server the type becomes 'serial' and the identity clause is skipped.
A 64-bit request (:Bignum) goes through type_literal_generic_bignum_symbol: 'bigserial' when column[:serial] (old server), otherwise 'bigint' (then the identity clause as above).

CRITICAL: if the column also has a :default, column_definition_default_sql still emits DEFAULT <value> but silently omits the GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY clause (condition !column[:default]); serial types never get the clause.

For schema inspection, Postgres schema_parse_table sets :auto_increment for a primary key column when its default starts with nextval or the attidentity flag is 'a' or 'd'; the generic guess in Database#schema (query.rb) only applies if the adapter did not set :auto_increment.

probes.query: On PostgreSQL and on MySQL, a migration file written in block style, with no explicit transaction directive and no transaction option passed to the migration runner, creates a table that also has an index. Which transaction or savepoint scope surrounds the migration body, and which surrounds each index statement, on each of the two databases? Name every place whose rule decides this, and say how the answer changes if the migration declares that it wants no transaction or the runner is told to use transactions explicitly.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: Migrator#checked_transaction (migration.rb) decides by precedence: the migrator's :use_transactions option if not nil, else the migration's own use_transactions (SimpleMigration default nil; MigrationDSL#no_transaction sets false, #transaction sets true; the old class-based Migration returns nil), else db.supports_transactional_ddl?; it then calls db.transaction(skip_transaction: use_trans == false).

Database#supports_transactional_ddl? is false by default (database/features.rb) and true for PostgreSQL (shared/postgres.rb; also MSSQL and Derby), so with defaults the PostgreSQL migration body runs inside a real transaction and the MySQL migration body runs with no transaction (skip_transaction).
Database#transaction (transactions.rb) with :skip_transaction just checks out a connection and yields it, opening no transaction or savepoint.

CRITICAL: create_table runs create_table_indexes_from_generator after the table statement, which wraps each index statement in transaction(savepoint: :only, skip_transaction: supports_transactional_ddl? == false); on PostgreSQL inside the migration's transaction that opens a savepoint per index (so a swallowed index error, ignore_index_errors/if_not_exists, does not abort the outer transaction).

On MySQL the index statements get no savepoint even though MySQL supports savepoints, because skip_transaction is true (no transactional DDL); on PostgreSQL with a no-transaction migration, :savepoint=>:only finds no surrounding transaction and simply yields without any savepoint.

probes.query: A team keeps a personal access token, not an OAuth token, for their self-hosted instance of the code-hosting service whose API takes such tokens in a dedicated header instead of the standard authorization header. The instance is not in Composer's built-in host list, and the token sits in the user-level credentials file. Trace: (1) the order in which credential sources are read for a project, and which source wins for the same host; (2) how the host comes to be treated as that service's host, and in what form the token is held in memory; (3) which function builds the request header from that in-memory form, which header name results, and which two network transports call it; (4) what happens when the server answers with an authorization failure for that token; (5) how the same stored credential is turned into URL credentials when a clone over HTTPS from that host fails.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: Credential sources are merged in this order: the global home config.json, the global auth.json and the COMPOSER_AUTH environment variable (Factory::createConfig); then the project's composer.json config, the auth.json beside it, and COMPOSER_AUTH again (Factory::createComposer). The environment variable is applied last, and a later source overrides an earlier one for the same host.

CRITICAL: BaseIO::loadConfiguration (called from Factory::createComposer on a full load) takes each gitlab-token entry, adds a host that is missing from gitlab-domains to that list implicitly (source label 'implicit-due-to-auth'), and stores the entry through checkAndSetAuthentication. A plain string token becomes username = the token and password = the literal marker 'private-token'; an object with username and token is stored as that pair with no marker.

BaseIO::checkAndSetAuthentication overwrites different credentials already held for a host and only prints a warning; BaseIO::loadConfiguration loads http-basic and bearer entries after gitlab-token, so those would replace the token for the same host.

AuthHelper::addAuthenticationOptions, for a host listed in gitlab-domains whose password is 'private-token', adds the header 'PRIVATE-TOKEN: <username>' (the 'oauth2' marker gives an Authorization Bearer header, 'gitlab-ci-token' gives JOB-TOKEN); it is called from CurlDownloader::initDownload and from RemoteFilesystem::getOptionsForUrl.

On a 401 or 403 answer CurlDownloader::isAuthenticatedRetryNeeded calls AuthHelper::promptAuthIfNeeded; in its gitlab-domains branch, because credentials with the private-token marker already exist for the host, it throws a TransportException ('Invalid credentials ... aborting') with the status code instead of prompting.

In Git::runCommand, after a plain clone fails for a host that matches gitlab-domains, a stored credential whose password is one of the markers 'private-token', 'oauth2' or 'gitlab-ci-token' is swapped into URL form https://<marker>:<token>@host/path; any other credential is used as username:password.

probes.author: r3x-composer-drafter
probes.query: A project's manifest has an entry in its scripts section whose name is not one of Composer's lifecycle event names and whose value is the fully qualified name of a class that extends the console framework's command class, rather than a shell string. Explain end to end how typing that name after the tool's name runs that class: when and where the entry becomes a registered command and in which circumstances that registration step is skipped altogether; what prevents a clash with a built-in command or with a lifecycle name; how the project's own classes are made loadable at that moment; and how the class gets invoked. Then say what differs when the same value is reached by referencing the entry from another script entry, or through the generic command that runs a named script.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: Application::doRun registers script commands only inside the non-proxy-command block and only when $mayNeedScriptCommand is true: plugin commands may be needed (command name not resolved, empty, list or help, or autocompletion), or the resolved name is the run-script command, or the typed name differs from the resolved built-in name. It reads composer.json directly with json_decode and loops over its 'scripts' keys.

A script name that equals a Script\ScriptEvents constant (checked with defined('Composer\Script\ScriptEvents::' . UPPER_SNAKE name)) is not registered as a command; a name for which $this->has() is already true is skipped with the warning 'would override a Composer command and has been skipped'.

Before instantiating the first script command, Application::doRun registers the project's own autoloader once ($projectLoaderRegistered): AutoloadGenerator::buildPackageMap, parseAutoloads and createLoader from the loaded root package, then register(false), so command classes from the project's autoload sections can be resolved.

CRITICAL: When the value is a string that names an existing subclass of the Symfony Command class, Application::doRun instantiates it with the script name as argument (new $dummy($script)), forces that name if the class defines a different one (with a warning), takes the description from scripts-descriptions, and adds it directly, so typing the name runs the class through the console application without the event dispatcher. Any other value (shell string, array, non-Command class) becomes a ScriptAliasCommand built with the scripts-aliases entry.

ScriptAliasCommand::execute sets COMPOSER_DEV_MODE and calls EventDispatcher::dispatchScript with the script name, the args and a 'script-alias-input' flag holding the raw input after the name; in EventDispatcher::doDispatch a string listener that contains a backslash, has no space and ends in 'Command' takes the isCommandClass branch, which builds a fresh console Application with that class as default command and runs it with the stored input; it refuses event names that are lifecycle constants ('You cannot bind ... to a Command class').

Referencing the entry with an at-sign reference from another script goes through the isComposerScript branch of doDispatch, which creates a new ScriptEvent and re-dispatches by name; RunScriptCommand::execute rejects lifecycle names not in its own allowed list, requires hasEventListeners, and dispatches with dispatchScript; there a class name that does not end in 'Command' falls to the final else branch and is executed as a shell command string.

probes.query: Third-party code can ask, at run time, which package versions are installed (the runtime installed-versions API). When Composer itself runs a project's plugins or scripts, that API has to read the project's data instead of the tool's own bundled copy, and the tool must not execute arbitrary code from the data file. Trace: where, and under which conditions, the tool preloads the project's data at start-up; how the data file's content is checked before it is evaluated and how relative paths inside it are fixed up; how the class's static state is replaced and what that does to its protection against listing one dataset twice; how it later enumerates data when several autoloaders from different vendor folders are registered; and where that data file and a copy of the class are first produced after an install, and how that writer synchronises the in-memory state.

CRITICAL: FilesystemRepository::safelyLoadInstalledVersions reads the file and proceeds only if a recursive regex matches the whole content as '<?php return array(...)' built from numbers, booleans/null, quoted strings (optionally concatenated) and nested arrays (with an optional __DIR__ . prefix on values); it then replaces '=> __DIR__ . ' with the exported dirname of the file path, evals the result into InstalledVersions::reload, and returns false (loads nothing) when the check fails.

InstalledVersions::reload replaces the static $installed data, empties $installedByVendor and sets $installedIsLocalDir to false, which disables the duplicate protection, so a later listing can contain the same dataset twice.

InstalledVersions::getInstalled, when ClassLoader::getRegisteredLoaders exists (the static map of registered loaders keyed by vendor dir, filled in ClassLoader::register), requires each registered vendor dir's composer/installed.php once (cached in $installedByVendor), avoids adding its own static copy a second time when it comes from the same directory (selfDir / installedIsLocalDir), and only requires its own installed.php when the class file is not located in a source checkout (the 'C' of 'Composer' at position -8 of __DIR__).

FilesystemRepository::write, when dumpVersions is on, builds the dataset with generateInstalledVersions, writes vendor/composer/installed.php via dumpToPhpCode (a relative install_path is emitted as a __DIR__ . '/...' concatenation), copies src/Composer/InstalledVersions.php to vendor/composer/InstalledVersions.php if readable, calls InstalledVersions::reload, then sets the private selfDir to the vendor/composer dir and installedIsLocalDir to true through reflection.

AutoloadGenerator::dump adds the class Composer\InstalledVersions to the class map with the path vendor/composer/InstalledVersions.php, so the copy inside the vendor folder is the one the project's autoloader serves.

probes.author: r3x-composer-drafter
probes.query: A project depends on packages published through a remote package index that uses the newer per-package metadata protocol. Trace what happens from the moment the dependency-pool builder asks its repositories for a batch of package names until the candidate versions come back: how repositories are queried in order and when a name found in one stops being asked of later ones; how a repository wrapper that restricts names, or that declares itself non-authoritative, changes that; how the index's root file tells the repository where the per-package files live and which names it can know; which extra companion file is requested for development versions; how the cached copy is revalidated and what the user sees when the server fails; how the compact version list is expanded; and which versions are finally accepted.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: PoolBuilder::loadPackagesMarkedForLoading splits the names into batches of 50 (LOAD_BATCH_SIZE), walks the repositories in priority order (skipping the platform repository and the locked repository), and removes every name returned in namesFound from the remaining batches, so lower-priority repositories are not asked for a name an earlier one already found.

FilterRepository::loadPackages drops names not allowed by its only/exclude patterns before delegating; when its canonical option is false it empties namesFound in the result, so later repositories are still queried for those names.

ComposerRepository::loadRootServerFile reads packages.json (cached copy, revalidated with its stored last-modified value) and, when it contains a metadata-url, treats the repository as the newer protocol: the URL pattern becomes lazyProvidersUrl, the legacy provider keys are discarded, and available-packages / available-package-patterns (if present) make the name list finite, so ComposerRepository::loadPackages drops unknown names through lazyProvidersRepoContains before fetching.

ComposerRepository::loadAsyncPackages also queues a '<name>~dev' file for each name for which dev stability is acceptable (and drops the plain file when only dev stability is acceptable), skips platform packages and the root package, and each file is fetched from the metadata-url with %package% replaced and cached under the key 'provider-<name with / replaced by ~>.json'.

CRITICAL: startCachedAsyncDownload/asyncFetchFile send If-Modified-Since from the cached last-modified value, treat 304 as 'use the cache', remember a 404 as an empty result, fire the pre/post file-download plugin events, and on any other failure print a warning once ('could not be fully loaded ... may be out of date', degraded mode) and, if a last-modified value exists, fake a 304 so the cached data is used, otherwise rethrow (a 499 'network disabled' error is turned into a not-found result).

When the response is marked minified ('composer/2.0') the version list is expanded with MetadataMinifier::expand; each version is then kept only if isVersionAcceptable passes: the version or its branch alias satisfies the stability rules (StabilityFilter) and the requested constraint, and it was not already loaded.

probes.author: r3x-composer-drafter
probes.query: Composer treats package metadata published by third parties as untrusted. List every place in production code where it defends against (a) a package's declared executable entries, or (b) a package's source or download location and revision strings, being abused to reach files outside the package folder, to be read by external tools as command-line switches, or to launch a local program. expectedFacts: CRITICAL: ValidatingArrayLoader::load rejects a bin entry (string or each array element) containing a '..' path component: it records an error and unsets that entry; it also records errors for a source/dist url or reference that starts with '-' (so it cannot be read as a command-line option by the VCS tooling).
ValidatingArrayLoader::load additionally validates a source url of type perforce with Perforce::isValidPort and records an error when it is not of the form [tcp|ssl:][host:]port.

CRITICAL: ValidatingArrayLoader::validatePackage re-applies the security subset to an already loaded package (package name structure, leading '-' on source/dist url and reference, perforce port, '..' in bin) and throws SecurityException; LockTransaction::setResultPackages calls it for every package the solver selects, so it also covers packages that were loaded by the non-validating ArrayLoader (root packages are exempt).

Perforce::isValidPort rejects any value starting with the rsh: or jsh: transport (which would make the p4 client run a local command) and accepts only an optional tcp/ssl transport, a host or bracketed address and an optional port; the Perforce constructor throws SecurityException for an invalid port, while checkServerExists just returns false.

BinaryInstaller::installBinaries skips a bin (printing a warning and continuing) when its resolved real path is outside the package's install directory, for example a symlink pointing out of the package; isBinPathInsidePackage compares realpath() of both paths and fails closed (false) if either cannot be resolved.

FileDownloader::install, for a single-file dist, only makes a declared bin executable (chmod) when BinaryInstaller::isBinPathInsidePackage is true and otherwise silently skips it (BinaryInstaller reports it later in the same install).

probes.author: r3x-composer-drafter
probes.query: A project has a lock file. A developer updates only one named dependency but also allows that package's own dependencies to move. One of those dependencies is also required directly by the project's own manifest, and another comes from a local-folder (linked) repository. Explain which dependencies are unlocked and which stay at their locked versions, what the user sees, and how the outcome changes with the stricter variant that also frees directly required dependencies. Include how the list of names given by the developer is matched, what happens when a listed name matches nothing, and what is refused when no lock file exists.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: UpdateCommand::execute maps the dependency options to Request constants: none -> UPDATE_ONLY_LISTED, the 'with dependencies' option -> UPDATE_LISTED_WITH_TRANSITIVE_DEPS_NO_ROOT_REQUIRE, the 'with all dependencies' option -> UPDATE_LISTED_WITH_TRANSITIVE_DEPS (checked first, so it wins); Installer::doUpdate refuses a partial update without a lock file (ERROR_NO_LOCK_FILE_FOR_PARTIAL_UPDATE) and passes list and mode to Request::setUpdateAllowList.

PoolBuilder::buildPool: every locked package whose name matches none of the listed patterns (BasePackage::packageNameToRegexp: case-insensitive, '*' wildcard) is recorded in skippedLoad (also under the names it replaces) and passed to Request::lockPackage, so only its locked version is loaded.

A locked package from a path repository (dist type 'path' with symlink not disabled) is not locked: it is recorded in pathRepoUnlocked and loaded from its repository, but loaded without update propagation, so its own dependencies are not unlocked by it; only if it is later unlocked as a dependency of an updated package is it reloaded with propagation.

probes.query: A developer depends on a package that lives in a local folder and is not fetched from a remote. The package's manifest has no version field. Explain which version label the package receives and in what order of precedence the possible sources are checked (an explicit per-package override in the repository definition, the manifest, an environment-level override of the root project's version, automatic detection from version control, and a last default), and what automatic detection returns when the folder is a checkout on a feature branch, on a detached head, or on a tagged commit. Then explain which value acts as the package's content revision marker and how it is derived, why editing that folder's manifest causes a refresh of the installed package on the next full update, and what a plain install from the existing lock file compares instead.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: PathRepository::initialize decides the version in this order: a version for the package name in the repository's options.versions overrides everything including the manifest; else the manifest version; else, if COMPOSER_ROOT_VERSION is set and the folder's HEAD commit equals the current project's HEAD, the root version from the environment (VersionGuesser::getRootVersionFromEnv); else VersionGuesser::guessVersion; else 'dev-main'.

VersionGuesser::guessGitVersion takes the current branch as 'dev-<branch>' (normalised); on a detached head it uses 'dev-<sha>' and then prefers a tag when versionFromGitTags (git describe --exact-match --tags) finds one; if the folder is not a git checkout, guessVersion falls through to the hg, fossil and svn guessers.

A branch is a feature branch unless it matches master|main|latest|next|current|support|tip|trunk|default|develop|a numeric dotted name, or one of the package's own non-feature-branches; for a feature branch (without a declared branch-alias, or when 'self.version' is used) guessFeatureVersion picks the nearest other non-feature branch by shortest 'git rev-list candidate..branch' output (local branches before remote, ties go to the later entry in natural-descending order, i.e. the older version branch), and PathRepository then registers two packages: the feature-branch version and the nearest-branch version.

The content revision marker (dist reference) is null when the reference option is 'none'; for 'config' or 'auto' it is sha1 of the manifest JSON text concatenated with serialize(options); for 'auto' with a .git directory and a successful git rev-list it is replaced by the HEAD commit hash.

CRITICAL: Transaction::calculateOperations creates an UpdateOperation for a present package when its version, dist reference, source reference, or abandonment information differs, so an edited manifest (new hash) makes the next full update, which re-reads the path repository and rewrites the lock, produce a different reference and therefore a refresh.

A plain install does not re-read the folder: Installer::doInstall builds a LocalRepoTransaction from the locked repository and the installed repository, so it compares the lock's recorded version and references with the installed record.

probes.query: A developer uses the project's command-line scaffolding program to generate a new request-gate (filter) class, passing an option that changes the ending of the generated source file names. Trace the full path: how the two words typed after the program name select the code that does the work, how that code obtains the boilerplate text it fills in, how that boilerplate text became part of the program at build time (name the program that converted it and the build rule that runs it), and where the changed file ending is stored and read. Give file and symbol for each step.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: exeCommand (drogon_ctl/cmd.cc) builds the registry name 'drogon_ctl::' + the first word, creates the handler through the class registry (DrClassMap::newObject), casts it to CommandHandler and calls handleCommand with the remaining words. main.cc passes the arguments on after stripping the file-extension flags.

create::handleCommand (drogon_ctl/create.cc) rewrites the second word to 'create_' + word and calls exeCommand again, so the second round resolves to drogon_ctl::create_filter, whose handleCommand writes the header and source files.

create_filter.cc obtains its boilerplate by calling DrTemplateBase::newTemplate with the names filter_h and filter_cc. newTemplate (lib/src/DrTemplateBase.cc) looks the name up in the class registry and returns a template object that is filled with class name, file name and both extensions.

CRITICAL: At build time drogon_ctl/CMakeLists.txt globs templates/*.csp and for each file runs a custom command that calls the helper executable _drogon_ctl (variable DROGON_CTL, set in the root CMakeLists.txt; a host-installed copy when cross-compiling) with 'create view <file>'. The generated .cc files are linked into the final drogon_ctl program.

create_view.cc names the generated class after the .csp file's base name and makes it derive from drogon::DrTemplate<Name>. DrObject's static DrAllocator registers each such class in DrClassMap under its type name, which is why the lookup by 'filter_cc' succeeds.

The file-ending option is parsed in main.cc into the global inline strings sourceExtension / headerExtension declared in drogon_ctl/extension.h. Their defaults come from compile definitions that drogon_ctl/CMakeLists.txt takes from root CMake cache variables. create_filter.cc uses them for the output file names and passes them to the templates.

probes.query: A controller class declares one of its methods with the class-level registration macro, giving a path pattern that contains a positional placeholder and naming one access-gate (filter) class by its string name. Trace the whole life of that declaration: what triggers registration before the program's main function runs, how the pattern becomes a lookup entry, when and how the gate's name becomes a live object, and how a request for a matching URL is first gated and then has its placeholder text turned into the typed method argument. Give file and symbol for each step.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: HttpController<T> has a static data member registrator_ of type methodRegistrator whose constructor calls T::initPathRouting() when auto-creation is enabled. Its static initialisation runs before main. initPathRouting is the function generated by the list-begin/list-end macros and holds the registerMethod calls.

registerMethod (HttpController.h) builds the route (for the class-relative macro: '/' + class name with '::' replaced by '/' + pattern) and calls app().registerHandler. The registerHandler template in HttpAppFramework.h splits the constraint list: HTTP-method values become valid methods, strings become middleware names. It then calls registerHttpController, which HttpAppFrameworkImpl forwards to HttpControllersRouter::addHttpPath.

addHttpPath rewrites each {..} placeholder into the capture group ([^/]*), records the positional index mapping in the binder's parameterPlaces_, and stores the binder either in ctrlMap_ keyed by the lower-cased exact path (no placeholders) or in ctrlVector_ (a regex entry, compiled later in init()).

CRITICAL: The filter name becomes a live object only when HttpControllersRouter::init runs from HttpAppFrameworkImpl::run (after plugin initialisation): createMiddlewares calls DrClassMap::getSingleInstance(name) and dynamic-casts to HttpMiddlewareBase. A filter qualifies because HttpFilterBase derives from HttpMiddlewareBase and its final invoke() adapts to doFilter. A name that fails the lookup is only logged and skipped, so the route runs without the gate.

At request time HttpServer::requestPassMiddlewares calls middlewares_function::passMiddlewares on the binder's middlewares after routing and post-routing advices and before pre-handling advices and the handler. The filter's response callback sends its response and stops the chain; its chain callback continues to the next middleware and finally the handler.

HttpControllersRouter::route matches ctrlMap_ first and then the ctrlVector_ regexes, writes the captures into the parameter list at the positions in parameterPlaces_ and calls setRoutingParameters. HttpControllerBinder::handleRequest copies them into a deque and HttpBinder::run converts each string with getHandlerArgumentValue (for example std::stoi for int); invalid_argument or out_of_range leads to handleBadPathParameter (HTTP 400).

probes.query: On the PostgreSQL backend, an application holds a database transaction object obtained from a pooled client. One statement is executing on it and two more statements are queued behind it on the same transaction. The executing statement fails on the server. Trace what happens next: what the failing statement's caller receives, what the two waiting callers receive and why they never reach the server, how the transaction is closed on the server, and the exact sequence of code by which the physical connection returns to the pool and what the pool does with it next. Give file and symbol for each step.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: PgConnection::handleRead sees an error result and calls handleFatalError, which invokes the statement's exception callback with the database error. TransactionImpl::execSqlInLoop wrapped that callback so that it first calls TransactionImpl::rollback() and then forwards the original error to the caller, who therefore receives the database failure (not a rollback exception).
rollback() finds the transaction still marked working, so it queues a 'rollback' command at the FRONT of sqlCmdBuffer_ (push_front, flagged isRollbackCmd_), ahead of the two waiting statements.

After the failed command, PgConnection::handleRead calls the connection's idle callback; TransactionImpl::doBegin installed it to call execNewTask. execNewTask pops the rollback command first and runs it on the connection; when it succeeds isCommitedOrRolledback_ becomes true.

CRITICAL: On the next idle callback execNewTask sees isCommitedOrRolledback_ true, clears isWorking_ and calls failBufferedCommands: each waiting statement's exception callback gets a TransactionRollback exception ('The transaction has been rolled back'), so they are never sent to the server.

execNewTask then calls releaseConnection, which runs usedUpCallback_ (built in DbClientImpl::makeTrans). Unless the connection is Bad or no longer in connections_, that callback queues work on the connection's loop that re-installs the pool's idle callback and calls DbClientImpl::handleNewTask.

handleNewTask serves the oldest pending transaction request in transCallbacks_ first (makeTrans again), otherwise the oldest buffered plain statement in sqlCmdBuffer_, otherwise moves the connection from busyConnections_ to readyConnections_.

probes.query: A browser asks the server to switch an existing connection to the persistent two-way messaging protocol, targeting a path served by a controller written for that protocol. Trace from the point where the connection-level request handler recognises the request as such an upgrade to the point where the controller's message handler runs for the first text message the browser sends afterwards. Cover: what is checked to recognise the upgrade, which routing and pre-handling stages it passes through (and which usual stages it skips), how the handshake reply is produced and sent, what keeps the link alive afterwards, and how later bytes on the same TCP connection are diverted away from the normal request parser. Give file and symbol for each step.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: HttpServer::onRequests treats a request as an upgrade only when exactly one request was parsed, nothing is pipelined, and isWebSocket is true: method GET, both Upgrade and Connection headers present, the Connection value contains 'upgrade' and the Upgrade value equals 'websocket' (case-insensitive). Otherwise it is routed as ordinary HTTP.

In that branch the sync advices run first, a WebSocketConnectionImpl is created and a ping with an empty payload every 30 seconds is scheduled (setPingMessage). Then onWebsocketRequest runs session lookup and pre-routing advices, websocketRequestRouting calls routeWs (NotFound unless a sec-websocket-key header is present; lower-cased path looked up in wsCtrlMap_, else regex entries in wsCtrlVector_), and the shared requestPostRouting runs post-routing advices, middlewares and requestPreHandling before websocketRequestHandling. The cached-response, static-file, request-decompression and response-compression steps are skipped.

WebsocketControllerBinder::handleRequest (HttpControllerBinder.cc) computes the accept value as base64 of the SHA-1 of the client key plus the fixed protocol GUID, and builds a 101 Switching Protocols response with Upgrade and Connection headers.

CRITICAL: The reply callback in onRequests applies session handling and pre-sending advices; only if the status is 101 does it call requestParser->setWebsockConnection(wsConn); it then sends the rendered response directly with conn->send(renderToBuffer()), bypassing the pipelining queue and handleResponse.

websocketRequestHandling then calls WebsocketControllerBinder::handleNewConnection, which installs the message callback (calls the controller's handleNewMessage) and the close callback (handleConnectionClosed) on the connection object and calls the controller's handleNewConnection.

For later bytes, HttpServer::onMessage checks requestParser->webSocketConn() first and hands the buffer to WebSocketConnectionImpl::onNewMessage, which parses frames, answers ping with pong, shuts the TCP connection down on a close frame, and calls the stored message callback for each message.

probes.query: List every place in the production code where a lost connection to an external peer (a relational database, a key-value cache server, or a remote persistent-messaging server) is opened again automatically after a timed wait, with no new application request needed to trigger it. For each place give the class or function and the length of the wait. Leave out places that only retry a command on a healthy connection, and say which database backend deliberately never gets a replacement connection.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: DbClientImpl::newConnection's close callback (orm_lib/src/DbClientImpl.cc) removes the closed connection from the pools and re-creates one after 1 second (loop->runAfter(1, ...)) for PostgreSQL and MySQL.

DbClientLockFree::newConnection's close callback (orm_lib/src/DbClientLockFree.cc) erases the connection and calls newConnection again after 1 second on the client's own loop (the per-I/O-thread fast client).

CRITICAL: SQLite is the exception: in the same DbClientImpl close callback the Sqlite3 branch increments failedSqliteConnections_, never schedules a replacement, and once all connections have failed it fails the queued commands and transactions with BrokenConnection.

PgListener::newConnection's close callback (orm_lib/src/postgresql_impl/PgListener.cc) reconnects after 2*retryCnt seconds for the first four failures and 10 seconds afterwards; retryCnt is reset to 0 when a connection succeeds. The LISTEN/UNLISTEN retries in listenInLoop use the same delay formula but retry a command with a maximum number of attempts and are not reconnects.

Redis: RedisClientImpl and RedisClientLockFree each schedule a replacement after 2.0 seconds from the disconnect callbacks of both newConnection (ordinary connection) and newSubscribeConnection (the subscribe variants re-attach the same subscriber): four sites in nosql_lib/redis/src.

probes.query: When an application running with default settings receives a termination signal, list in order every step the framework performs to stop, from the signal to the point where the event loops are told to end. Include the steps that happen indirectly inside the destructors of the subsystems the framework owns and say what each of those does. Name which subsystem is stopped first, and say which owned subsystems are NOT released as part of this sequence but only later.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: HttpAppFrameworkImpl::run installs the C signal handler TERMFunction for SIGINT and SIGTERM when signal handling is enabled (the default); it logs and calls the configurable term / int signal handler, whose default lambdas (HttpAppFrameworkImpl.h) call app().quit().
quit() acts only if the main loop is running and running_ flips from true to false (exchange), then queues all its work onto the main loop.

CRITICAL: The first subsystem stopped is the listeners: ListenerManager::stopListening stops every HttpServer (on non-Linux builds it also quits and joins the dedicated listening thread) and the listener manager is then reset, despite the comment saying 'reverse order of initialization'.
Next StaticFileRouter::reset and HttpControllersRouter::reset clear the routing state (static locations and caches, controller maps).

Then pluginsManagerPtr_.reset() runs ~PluginsManager, which calls shutdown() on every initialised plugin in the reverse of initialisation order; then redisClientManagerPtr_.reset() runs ~RedisClientManager and dbClientManagerPtr_.reset() runs ~DbClientManager, each calling closeAll on named clients and closing the per-I/O-thread fast clients on their own loops through a promise/future.

Last, the main loop quits, every I/O loop quits and ioLoopThreadPool_->wait() blocks. The shared-library (dynamic view) manager and the session manager are not released here but only in ~HttpAppFrameworkImpl.

probes.query: An operator sets up encrypted listening in the application's JSON configuration: a global section with a certificate file, a key file and a list of low-level TLS option commands, plus one listener that is marked encrypted but supplies only its own key file and its own extra TLS option commands (no certificate). Which certificate and key does that listener finally use, which TLS option commands does it get, at what point does the process fail if something is missing, and does the answer depend on the operating system the server runs on? Give file and function for each part of the decision.
expectedFacts: Loading the configuration only stores values: ConfigLoader::loadSSL calls setSSLFiles / setSSLConfigCommands (members sslCertPath_, sslKeyPath_, sslConfCmds_) and loadListeners calls addListener, which stores each listener's own cert, key, old-TLS flag and option commands. Nothing is merged at load time.

The merge happens in HttpAppFrameworkImpl::run, which passes the three global values to ListenerManager::createListeners after the I/O thread pool exists and before DB clients, plugins and routers are set up.

CRITICAL: Certificate and key fall back independently to the global values (an empty listener cert takes the global cert, an empty listener key takes the global key), so a listener with only its own key uses the global certificate together with its own key.

If cert or key is still empty after the fallback, createListeners prints 'You can't use https without cert file or key file' to stderr and calls exit(1) at startup (not at config load). This is evaluated only for listeners marked encrypted and when TLS support is compiled in.

CRITICAL: Option commands are OS dependent: the Linux branch of createListeners builds the list as the global commands followed by the listener's own (std::copy with back_inserter); the non-Linux branch uses only the global commands and silently ignores the listener's own commands.
The old-TLS flag comes only from the listener (policy->setUseOldTLS(listener.useOldTLS_)) on both branches; there is no global value for it.

An application's JSON configuration lists, in this order, a PostgreSQL database client (with a database name) and a cache-server client. probes.query: On a database pool with several reader connections, an app runs its schema-migration helper at launch. The helper is set to start over from an empty file whenever the schema definitions no longer match what the database was built with. Trace the whole path. How does the pool make sure no reader is mid-read? How does the helper decide that the definitions changed: where does it run the comparison, what does that scratch copy inherit from the real connection, and which schema objects are left out of the comparison? How is the file finally emptied in a standard build, and how in a build that links the encryption extension?
expectedFacts: The migrator entry point runs inside writer.barrierWriteWithoutTransaction. On a pool, that method wraps writer.sync in readerPool.barrier, and Pool.barrier waits (itemsGroup.wait on a barrier-flagged queue) until no reader is in use, before any reader is handed out again.

The private migrate(db, upTo:) acts only when the erase-on-schema-change option is on: it calls hasSchemaChanges inside a deferred transaction, and only if that returns true (after the transaction) it calls db.erase(); the normal migration run follows in all cases.

CRITICAL: hasSchemaChanges returns true at once if the applied migration identifiers are not a subset of the registered ones. Otherwise, if at least one registered migration was applied, it migrates a temporary on-disk database (unique name in the temp directory) up to the last applied identifier and compares that database main schema with the real one. If no registered migration was applied, it returns false.
The scratch database uses a copy of the real connection configuration, with readonly turned off, target queue and write target queue cleared (to avoid deadlocks), and a temporary label.

The comparison skips schema objects whose names start with the SQLite internal prefixes (sqlite_, pragma_) or with grdb_ (isSQLiteInternalTable / isGRDBInternalTable); SchemaObject equality covers type, name, table name and the SQL text.

CRITICAL: Database.erase() in a standard build copies an empty in-memory DatabaseQueue onto the connection through the backup API (DatabaseReader.backup(to: Database) reads the source and calls Database.backupInternal, which then clears the destination schema cache). With SQLITE_HAS_CODEC it calls dropAllDatabaseObjects instead, because SQLCipher lacks the backup API: foreign keys are switched off if on, every object not named sqlite_% is dropped in one transaction, and foreign keys are restored.

probes.query: An app fetches books together with their authors in one joined query, where the author may be missing (outer join), into a decodable struct that holds a book and an optional author. Trace how one flat result row becomes a base row plus a named author sub-row. How does the library learn where the author's columns start and end inside the flat row (what does it consult to count them), what object slices the row at fetch time, and how does the decoder conclude that the optional author is absent when the outer join found nothing? What changes if the property were not optional?
expectedFacts: SQLQualifiedJoin turns an optional to-one child into LEFT JOIN and a required one into JOIN. Both selected tables sit in one SELECT. QueryInterfaceRequest.makePreparedRequest asks SQLQueryGenerator for the statement and for a row adapter (nil when the root relation has no join).

CRITICAL: SQLQualifiedRelation.rowAdapter walks the join tree with a running start index. Each relation width is its selection column count: SQLSelection.columnCount asks SQLGenerationContext.columnCount, which returns the count of Database.columns(in:) for the table (minus excluded columns) or the CTE column count. Literal selections cannot be counted.

Each relation gets RangeRowAdapter(start ..< start+width). Joined relations adapters are stored under the join key (the association name) and attached with addingScopes, which wraps them in a ScopeAdapter. The range adapter hides the appended joined columns from the base row.

At fetch time RowCursor.init (used by Row.fetchAll and the record fetch paths) builds the statement row and calls adapted(with:layout: statement). ScopeAdapter._layoutedAdapter lays out the base mapping and each scope mapping, producing an AdaptedRowImpl whose scopes view exposes the author sub-row (Row.scopes / scopesTree).

CRITICAL: In the keyed decoding container, decodeIfPresent looks for a column first, then a scope: if the scoped row containsNonNullValue (which also inspects nested scopes) it decodes it, otherwise it returns nil. So an all-NULL outer-join row gives a nil optional author.

The non-optional decode(_:forKey:) scope branch decodes the scoped row without any null check, so an all-NULL author row is decoded as a record and normally fails on its non-null columns. The lookup order is column, then scope, then prefetched rows.
