probes.query: A parent record is fetched together with all of its children through the library's eager-loading option for to-many associations, and the children end up in an array property of a decodable struct. The link between the two tables spans two columns. Trace the path from the request to the filled array. Where is the second query attached and run, what does it filter on when the link has several columns (and why does the library avoid putting the parent values in the filter), how are children matched back to each parent, and which decoding code reads them out? Which fetch style is not supported with this option?
expectedFacts: QueryInterfaceRequest.makePreparedRequest attaches a supplementary-fetch closure to the PreparedRequest when the relation has prefetched (to-many) associations. The main SQL has no join for them: SQLQualifiedJoin returns nil for the all and bridge child kinds.

Row.fetchAll(db, request) fetches the base rows first, then calls the supplementary closure with those rows. Row.fetchCursor with such a request hits a precondition (not implemented), so cursor-style fetching is the unsupported style.

The private prefetch function returns early when there are no base rows. For each association it gets the foreign key join mapping (SQLForeignKeyCondition.joinMapping), giving the origin (left) columns and the child pivot (right) columns.

CRITICAL: With a single-column link the child query is filtered with an IN list of the distinct non-NULL parent values (JoinMapping.joinExpression(leftRows:)). With a multi-column link it instead injects the base request as a common table expression named grdb_base (unordered unless limited, prefetches removed, only the link columns selected) and filters on a row-value IN against it, to avoid the SQLite expression-tree depth limit from long OR/AND chains.

makePrefetchRequest annotates each child row with its pivot column values under grdb_<column> aliases. Child rows are grouped by those values, and each base row receives its group through PrefetchedRowsView.setRows(forKeyPath: association key path) using the left column values.

CRITICAL: In the keyed decoding container, after checking column and scope, the key is looked up in row.prefetchedRows; if present a PrefetchedRowsDecoder feeds the unkeyed array decoding of the children.

probes.query: In a table-creation block, a developer adds a to-one reference to another table by giving only a bare name, with no table named. Trace from the table-creation call to the generated SQL. How does the library pick the referenced table, including a name that does not match a table exactly and a reference from a table to itself? What columns does it add, how are their names and types derived from the referenced table's key (consider an implicit row id, a single-column key and a composite key), and what constraint and index come out in each case?
expectedFacts: Database.create(table:) runs the body to collect a TableDefinition, builds SQLTableGenerator(db, table:), then executes generator.sql(db). belongsTo only records a ForeignKeyDefinition (name, optional table, actions, deferred flag); it is indexed by default unless used inside a primary-key body, where it is forced NOT NULL and not indexed.

CRITICAL: Referenced table choice (ForeignKeyDefinition.primaryKey): the explicit table if given; else a table named exactly like the bare name if it exists; else the pluralized name (Inflections.pluralized) if that table exists; else DatabaseError.noSuchTable.

Self reference: makeForeignKeyGenerator treats the reference as auto-referencing when the origin table equals the given table (case-insensitive), or, when no table is given, when the singularized origin table name equals the singularized bare name. It then uses the forward-declared primary key columns of the table being defined, because that table does not yet exist in the schema.

CRITICAL: Column shape follows the key of the referenced table (SQLPrimaryKeyDescriptor.find via db.primaryKey(table).columnInfos, nil for a hidden row id): implicit row id gives one column <name>Id of type INTEGER with REFERENCES table; a single-column key gives <name><KeyColumn with first letter uppercased> with the key column declared type and REFERENCES table(keyColumn); a composite key gives one column per key column (same naming and types) plus a table-level FOREIGN KEY ... REFERENCES table (key columns looked up from the schema).

Indexing: for single-column references the column is marked indexed (index named <table>_on_<column>, created by the column generator) or unique (inline UNIQUE, no separate index); for composite references a separate SQLIndexGenerator named index_<table>_on_<col1>_<col2> (unique if requested) is generated.

probes.query: Besides the application's own databases, the library sometimes opens a private, short-lived connection of its own, either to ask SQLite a question or to obtain a clean empty file. Name every library operation that does this. For each, say what the scratch connection is used for and whether it lives in memory or on disk. Do not count public helpers whose purpose is to hand a copy to the caller, or internal connections that point at the application's own database file.
expectedFacts: Database.sqliteCompileOptions opens an in-memory DatabaseQueue and reads PRAGMA COMPILE_OPTIONS to list how SQLite was built (Database.swift:322-326).

Database.erase (standard build) uses an empty in-memory DatabaseQueue as the backup source that is copied over the connection (Database.swift:1836-1842); the SQLCipher build drops objects instead and opens no scratch connection.

FTS3.tokenize and FTS5.tokenize(query:) each open an in-memory DatabaseQueue to run a tokenizer (an fts3tokenize virtual table queried by input; the FTS5 tokenizer made from the ascii descriptor, colocated tokens dropped).

CRITICAL: FTS3Pattern.init(rawPattern:) and FTS5Pattern.init(rawPattern:allowedColumns:) each open an in-memory DatabaseQueue, create a throwaway virtual table, and run a MATCH query to let SQLite validate the pattern; the thrown DatabaseError is rebuilt without private SQL and arguments.

CRITICAL: DatabaseMigrator.hasSchemaChanges is the only scratch connection on disk: a DatabaseQueue at a unique temporary-directory path (deleted afterwards), configured like the real database but writable, used to replay migrations and compare schemas.
Not counted: DatabaseQueue.inMemoryCopy and temporaryCopy (public copy helpers), and DatabaseSnapshotPool holder connections (they open the application file path to hold a WAL snapshot).

probes.query: The library caches knowledge about table layouts (columns, keys, indexes) per connection. Name every place where the library detects that this cached knowledge may be stale, or drops it, and say what triggers each. Cover a reader connection in a pool whose file was changed through the writer, the connection that itself runs a statement that changes the schema, and any explicit or helper paths. Also say what else is thrown away together with the cache.
expectedFacts: CRITICAL: Database.clearSchemaCacheIfNeeded compares PRAGMA schema_version (the 4-byte counter in the file header) with lastSchemaVersion and calls clearSchemaCache only when it changed.

CRITICAL: DatabasePool calls it on the reader connection at the start of every read flavour: read (sync and async variants), asyncRead, unsafeRead (sync and async), asyncUnsafeRead, unsafeReentrantRead (when it takes a pooled reader), and the concurrent-read start, where the same call doubles as the first SELECT that establishes snapshot isolation. WALSnapshotTransaction.init does it right after BEGIN DEFERRED.

On the connection that runs the change itself (the writer), staleness is detected per statement: StatementAuthorizer sets invalidatesDatabaseSchemaCache for DROP, CREATE, ALTER, ATTACH and DETACH action codes, and for the internal drop-column function on SQLite older than 3.38; Database.statementDidExecute then calls clearSchemaCache.
Database.withSchemaSource clears the cache both before running its block and after it (in defer), so information loaded through either schema source does not linger.
Database.backupInternal clears the schema cache of the destination connection when the copy finishes.
clearSchemaCache also empties the internal and public prepared-statement caches, because automatic statement recompilation is limited in the number of retries.

probes.query: An app watches the result of a query over a table of players. Watcher A filters on the integer key being in a short list AND on another column. Watcher B filters on the key being in a short list OR on another column. Watcher C is like A but runs over a table whose key is a text column. After a commit that modifies one player outside the list, which watchers fetch again, and why? Explain how the library narrows what a watcher cares about to specific rows: where the area is recorded, which filter shapes qualify, what is checked about the key column, what is never narrowed, and how a change event is finally compared with the narrowed area.
expectedFacts: The area is recorded while the watcher fetches: Database.statementWillExecute calls registerAccess(statement.databaseRegion), and SQLQueryGenerator.makeStatement has already narrowed that statement region by calling optimizedSelectedRegion before returning the statement.

CRITICAL: optimizedSelectedRegion narrows only when the source is a real table (views are skipped) and the filter has identifyingRowIDs; it then calls region.tableIntersection(table, rowIds). Only the source table is narrowed: joined tables and prefetched-children regions stay unbounded.

identifyingRowIDs: equality and IN on the row-id column with constant values give those ids; AND intersects the ids of the conjuncts that identify rows and ignores the others (so A is narrowed to the list); OR is the union only when every disjunct identifies rows, otherwise nil/unbounded (so B watches the whole table); constant NULL or false gives the empty set; any other shape is nil.

CRITICAL: A column counts as the row id only if Database.columnIsRowID: it equals the primary key rowIDColumn (a single-column key whose declared type is exactly INTEGER) or it is the literal rowid name on a rowid table. A text key, composite key or WITHOUT ROWID table is not recognised, so C is not narrowed and watches the whole table.

Event matching: DatabaseRegion.isModified(by: event) returns true when the event table is not in the region (for example unadvertised shadow-table changes of virtual tables); otherwise it returns TableRegion.contains(rowID), where nil rowIds means all rows. ValueConcurrentObserver.databaseDidChange(with:) marks the observation modified only if that returns true.
Result for the scenario: only watcher A ignores the commit; B and C fetch again because their area is the whole table.

probes.query: A struct record type declares its persistence settings so that updates silently skip a row that would break a constraint, while inserts replace conflicting rows. The app then saves a value whose key matches an existing row, but the new column values would break a uniqueness rule on another column. Walk through what the library does: which statements it sends, why the first step raises no database error, which internal condition it detects and swallows, what runs next, and the order in which the record's lifecycle callbacks fire.
expectedFacts: save runs willSave, then aroundSave wrapping updateOrInsertWithCallbacks, then didSave. updateOrInsertAndFetchWithCallbacks first reads the primary key values from the persistence container; if they are not all NULL it attempts an update using all table columns, otherwise it goes straight to insert.

The update goes through updateAndFetchWithCallbacks: willUpdate, aroundUpdate wrapping updateAndFetchWithoutCallbacks, didUpdate. The conflict resolution is the explicit argument or else the type persistenceConflictPolicy.conflictResolutionForUpdate (both default to abort), which DAO.updateStatement turns into UPDATE OR <resolution> table SET non-key columns WHERE key (no OR clause for abort).

CRITICAL: With the ignore resolution SQLite skips the violating row without error, so the UPDATE changes zero rows. updateAndFetchWithoutCallbacks measures changes through Database.countChanges (sqlite3_changes for tables) and, when the count is 0, throws RecordError.recordNotFound(table, key) via DAO.recordNotFound.

CRITICAL: updateOrInsertAndFetchWithCallbacks catches only recordNotFound with the same table name and key and then falls through to insertAndFetchWithCallbacks, which uses the insert resolution from the type policy (replace here): INSERT OR REPLACE INTO table. So a skipped update is treated like a missing row.
Callback order for this path: willSave, willUpdate, (aroundUpdate entered and left by the thrown error, so didUpdate never runs), willInsert, aroundInsert around the insert, didInsert, didSave.
